places.name: Bismarck, ND

visits.text: Start at the North Dakota Heritage Center and State Museum on the capitol grounds - North Dakota's largest museum and one of the best free museums on the Northern Plains. The 2014 expansion doubled it to 127,000 square feet across four galleries. The paleontology hall holds a life-size T. rex cast, but the showstopper is Dakota - a mummified Edmontosaurus discovered in 1999 near Marmarth, ND, and housed at the Heritage Center since 2008. Dakota is one of only a dozen fully mummified dinosaurs known to science, preserving extensive fossilized skin intact. The Early Peoples gallery displays over 1,000 artifacts from the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara nations. Free admission every day.

Drive 7 miles south to Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park, North Dakota's oldest state park, established in 1907 when Theodore Roosevelt signed over the land. Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer commanded the 7th Cavalry here from 1873 until he left for the Little Bighorn campaign in May 1876. At its height the fort held 650 men across 78 buildings; all were dismantled by settlers after its 1891 abandonment. The reconstructed Custer House is furnished as it would have been when Custer and his wife Libbie lived there. The On-A-Slant Village - a reconstruction of a Mandan earthlodge settlement occupied from around 1575 until a smallpox epidemic in the 1780s - completes the picture of who lived here before the fort arrived. Paid entry.

Walk the Missouri River waterfront at Keelboat Park, where a full-size replica of the Lewis and Clark keelboat sits at the river's edge. The Missouri at Bismarck is wide, brown, and powerful - the highway of exploration and westward expansion for two centuries. A statue of Sakakawea faces west, the direction she guided the Corps of Discovery. The state capitol dome rises just behind you. Free access.

activities.text: Take the self-guided tour of the North Dakota State Capitol - a 19-story Art Deco tower completed in 1934, the tallest building in either Dakota. The observation deck on the 18th floor gives a 360-degree view over the Missouri River valley and the rolling farmland. The guided tour covers the legislative chambers, murals, and the memorial hall. Free admission; observation deck closes at 4:30pm on weekdays.

Spend the evening in Bismarck's downtown around Main Avenue, where Laughing Sun Brewing and several other local spots sit alongside restaurants serving Northern Plains comfort food. If this is the last night of the road trip, it's a good place to eat well and look back at the week: a thousand-mile arc through battlefields, badlands, dinosaur bones, and the two states where the American West still feels most like itself.

visits.text: Columbus - The "Athens of the Prairie." This town of 47,000 inhabitants harbors more than 60 modernist buildings signed by world-renowned architects. In 1954, the Cummins Foundation began paying architect fees for public buildings - provided they chose among the best. Result: schools, churches, and banks designed by I.M. Pei, Eero Saarinen, or Robert Venturi. Stop by the Visitors Center on 5th Street for a walking tour map.

North Christian Church (Columbus) - The last building designed by Eero Saarinen before his death in 1961, completed in 1964. A stone hexagon topped by a 59-meter spire crowned with a golden cross. The interior receives natural light through a central oculus.

Nashville and Brown County - Continuing west, Nashville is an artists' village nestled in the wooded hills of Brown County. Galleries and shops line the main street. The atmosphere is relaxed - it's the kind of place where you stop for coffee and stay two hours.

Brown County State Park - Indiana's largest state park (6,500 hectares), 20 minutes from Nashville and 30 minutes from Bloomington where you'll sleep tonight. The scenic route overlooks offer views of forested ridges. In October, autumn colors attract crowds - arrive early if you're there during that period.

Indiana University Bloomington - IU's campus is one of the Midwest's most beautiful. Enter through the Sample Gates on Kirkwood Avenue, cross the lawns bordered by buildings in local limestone, and descend to the Jordan River (a creek, not a river). The Jacobs School of Music is one of the nation's finest - check if there's a free concert during your visit.

Marengo Cave - 45 minutes south of Bloomington, this cave designated a U.S. National Natural Landmark offers two underground routes: the "Dripstone Trail" (40 min, easy, family-friendly) and "Crystal Palace" (1h, more varied, with stalactites, stalagmites, and calcite columns). The formations were discovered in 1883 by two local children. Underground temperature is constant at 13°C - bring a sweater.

Spring Mill State Park - Halfway between Bloomington and Marengo, this park houses a reconstructed pioneer village with a working water mill. The Gus Grissom memorial (local native, died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967) displays his Gemini III "Molly Brown" space capsule.

activities.text: Guided tour of the Miller House (Columbus) - Eero Saarinen's 1957 private residence for the Miller family is one of the rare examples of a single-family home signed by the architect. Interiors by Alexander Girard, gardens by Dan Kiley. The "conversation pit" recessed into the living room floor became a model copied everywhere in the '60s. Tour by reservation only.

Bloomington Farmers Market (Saturday morning) - If you're there on the right day, the Showers Common market gathers local producers, cheesemakers, and artisan bakeries. The rest of the week, Kirkwood Avenue between campus and downtown abounds with bookstores, cafes, and restaurants from around the world - the international student population is reflected in the menus.

places.name: Bloomington, MN

visits.text: Mall of America—The largest shopping mall in the United States: 520 stores, an indoor amusement park with roller coasters (Nickelodeon Universe), an aquarium, and a mini-city. Even if shopping doesn't appeal to you, the spectacle of this outsized place is worth seeing. Allow at least 2 hours.

Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge—Ten minutes from the Mall, the scenery shifts dramatically. Take the trails through this 14,000-acre refuge along the Minnesota River—you might spot bald eagles, herons, and migrating pelicans. Free admission.

activities.text: If you're traveling with family, the indoor amusement park at Mall of America easily fills half a day. For adults, the craft breweries on the south side of the Mall offer an alternative to shopping.

places.name: Blowing Rock, NC

visits.text: Scale the legendary Blowing Rock, the high-altitude rock formation for which this scenic Blue Ridge Parkway town was named. This unique natural wonder features gusty winds so powerful they seem to return cast objects to the thrower, while the summit delivers unbeatable panoramic views of the surrounding mountain landscapes.

Embrace the challenge of hiking Glen Burney Falls Trail, a strenuous 1.6-mile outback route that rewards adventurers with the discovery of gorgeous waterfalls at trail's end. This wilderness adventure exemplifies the exceptional outdoor experiences available in this beautiful mountain destination.

activities.text: Explore local heritage at the Blowing Rock Art & History Museum, a celebrated center exhibiting diverse artworks that illuminate the overall heritage of Southern Appalachia. The museum's collections provide fascinating insight into the cultural traditions and artistic expressions that have shaped this mountain region for generations.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: From Outer Banks Beaches to Blue Ridge Mountains

map_keywords: Blowing Rock Art and History Museum

visits.text: Cave of the Mounds - This limestone cave is 488 million years old. Discovered in 1939 during a quarry blasting operation, it remained intact and contains remarkable formations: stalactites, stalagmites, helictites (growing in all directions), and soda straws (hollow, translucent formations). The guided tour lasts about one hour and the underground temperature is constant at 50°F - bring a jacket.
Surface Karst Trail - Above the cave, a trail through restored prairie explains the region's karst geology: sinkholes, fissures, and underground water circulation. Well-designed and educational.

Blue Mound State Park - Southern Wisconsin's highest point (1,710 feet). Two observation towers offer views across the Driftless Area - this Wisconsin region never covered by glaciers that retained unique rolling topography.

activities.text: Driftless Area Hiking - Blue Mound's trails cross wildflower prairies and oak forests. The contrast with the flat lands of the rest of the Midwest is striking.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: En route south, stop at Newspaper Rock—a 15-square-foot petroglyph panel covered with over 650 carvings accumulated over 2,000 years by Fremont, Ancestral Puebloan, and Ute peoples. The site is right by the roadside, 12 miles off Highway 191 on the road to Needles. Free and open access.

Don't underestimate Bluff—this tiny village of 250 people on the San Juan River, surrounded by red cliffs. The Bluff Fort Historic Site tells the story of Mormon pioneers' arrival in 1880, after an epic expedition through a gap in the cliff called Hole-in-the-Rock. It's also the gateway to Bears Ears National Monument—sacred land to the Navajo, Hopi, Ute, and Zuni nations.

activities.text: If you have time, do the Valley of the Gods loop (17 miles of dirt road, passable in regular car in dry weather). It's Monument Valley in miniature—isolated buttes and mesas, no tourists and no entrance fee. Allow 1-1.5 hours for the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Utah-Arizona Road Trip: National Parks and Canyons

visits.text: Mission San Francisco Solano, Sonoma Plaza: the 21st and last of California's Franciscan missions, founded in 1823. It's the last of California's 21 Franciscan missions, founded in 1823, and mission viticulture persisted here until the secularization of 1834 - the prehistory of everything you've been drinking these past four days. The current building dates largely to 1840. Small museum, $3 admission, 30 minutes is enough to understand the context.

Buena Vista Winery, 18000 Old Winery Road: founded in 1857 by Agoston Haraszthy, self-proclaimed count and Hungarian winemaker who brought back over 100,000 cuttings of European grape varieties to California in the 1860s. It's California's oldest commercial winery still in operation. The original stone building was restored in 2011 by Jean-Charles Boisset, Burgundian owner (DeLoach, Raymond in Napa). The place's history is more interesting than the wines - but the wines are decent.

Gundlach Bundschu, 2000 Denmark Street: founded in 1858, it's been in the same family for six generations - an absolute record in California. Less touristy than Buena Vista, more rural, intact family estate spirit. The quality-price ratio is one of Sonoma County's best. The Gewurztraminer and Pinot Noir are the two cuvées to ask for.

Bodega Bay and the Bodega School: the fishing village where Hitchcock shot The Birds in 1963. The Bodega School (17110 Bodega Lane), a red and white school on its hill, appears as-is in the film - you can stop on the road to photograph it, it's still operating. The village is unpretentious: fishing boats, crab restaurants, ocean fog.

activities.text: Lunch at The Girl & the Fig, Sonoma Plaza: Provençal-California cuisine founded in 1997 and now a local institution. The menu changes with market arrivals, wine is almost exclusively Rhône (French side) and Sonoma (local side). Book the day before for lunch.

Dinner at Spud Point Crab Co., Bodega Bay: clam chowder served in a sourdough bread bowl, Dungeness crab sandwich caught that morning. No fuss, no reservation, no pretense - exactly what's needed after two days of starred tastings. Count on $15-20 per person.

days_plan.itin_title: California Wine Country in 10 Days: San Francisco to Los Angeles Through the Vineyards

visits.text: Grove Street in downtown Boise is a single block that packs in the largest Basque community in North America - an estimated 16,000 residents whose ancestors left the Pyrenees in the late 1800s to herd sheep across Idaho's mountains. The cornerstone is the Cyrus Jacobs-Uberuaga House, built in 1864 and Boise's oldest surviving brick building; it served as a Basque boarding house from 1910 to 1968 and is now part of the Basque Museum & Cultural Center. The 1914 Anduiza Fronton next door still hosts handball and pala. Bar Gernika, opened in 1991 in a former 1912 Chinese laundromat, is the place for a pintxo and a glass of txakoli. The block is free to walk; the museum charges a small fee and closes on Sundays.

Steel doors clang shut behind you at the Old Idaho Penitentiary, and the sandstone walls - quarried by the inmates themselves from nearby Table Rock starting in 1872 - close in. The prison ran for exactly 101 years, housing over 13,000 people, including Harry Orchard, who assassinated Governor Frank Steunenberg in 1905 with a bomb wired to his front gate. Back-to-back riots in 1971 and 1973 burned the chapel and dining hall; the place closed in December 1973 and was left exactly as it stood that day, calendars still on the walls. Summer guided tours run daily from 10 AM to 5 PM for a fee - go at opening to avoid the wait.

Between 8th and 9th Street downtown lies Freak Alley - the Northwest's largest open-air mural gallery, born in 2002 when local artist Colby Akers painted a single alley doorway and the neighboring businesses asked for more. The project has since swallowed an entire city block and a gravel parking lot, with contributions from more than 200 artists. A $500,000 city renovation in 2018 expanded the space. Every August the murals are painted over during a week-long event and the whole thing starts again. Free and open 24 hours.

The Idaho State Capitol on Jefferson Street was completed in 1920 and is the only state capitol in the United States heated by geothermal water, drawn from a 3,000-foot well directly beneath the building. The interior dome rises 208 feet and is lined with four types of marble, including local Boise Basin stone. Self-guided tours are free on weekdays - check capitol.idaho.gov for guided tour times if you want the full context.

Julia Davis Park on the south bank of the Boise River holds the Idaho State Museum (rebuilt and reopened 2018), the Boise Art Museum, and the Idaho Anne Frank Human Rights Memorial - a free outdoor installation of granite walls engraved with human rights quotations, set among cottonwoods along the river. Thomas Davis donated the land in 1907 in memory of his wife. The park sits between downtown and Boise State University, which means it's lively on weekdays and a genuine retreat on weekend mornings.

Climb the bell tower of the Boise Depot at 2603 W Eastover Terrace and you're at the second-tallest point in the city, with views over the foothills and on clear days, the Sawtooth peaks 100 miles northeast. Built by Union Pacific in 1925 in Spanish Colonial Revival style, this was the terminal where Harriman's express trains unloaded Hollywood celebrities bound for Sun Valley. It's now a free public space; the building itself is worth the visit for the tile work alone.

activities.text: Rent a bike or lace up your shoes and head to the Boise River Greenbelt - 29 miles of paved path tracing both banks of the river through the heart of the city. The trail was born in 1967 from three donated parcels of land; the 1971 Greenbelt Ordinance forced new buildings to set back at least 70 feet from the riverbank, protecting the corridor you're on today. The stretch between Ann Morrison Park and Barber Park is the most scenic, with great blue herons working the shallows in the early morning. Bike rentals are available from several downtown outfitters.

The Basque Block alone gives you two dinner options: Leku Ona, a boutique hotel and restaurant opened in 2005 inside a historic boarding house, and Bar Gernika, where the beef tongue sandwich sells out by noon on Saturdays. For a broader choice, the 8th Street strip packs in everything from wood-fired pizza to craft cocktails within a few blocks. Book ahead for dinner in summer - Boise fills fast in July.

Rent a tube at Barber Park and float 5.5 miles back through the cottonwood corridor of the Boise River Greenbelt to Ann Morrison Park - 2 to 3 hours depending on current, with great blue herons overhead and the city skyline in the background. The water comes from Lucky Peak Reservoir and runs cold; late June through August is the sweet spot. Tube rentals and shuttles back to Barber Park operate on summer weekends from the downstream parks.

The loop closes on 8th Street, where Bittercreek Alehouse has been serving locally sourced Idaho food and regional craft beer since 1997. For a Basque send-off, Bar Gernika is open for lunch Tuesday through Saturday - the lamb sandwich and a Basque cider is the right order. Book a late-afternoon flight from BOI. Nine days and Idaho still has more to give.

places.name: Boone, NC

visits.text: Challenge yourself at Rocky Knob Mountain Bike Park, a popular recreation haven spreading over 180 acres with trails designed for all skill levels. This premier destination for hikers and bikers offers exciting outdoor opportunities amid the picturesque Blue Ridge Mountain landscape that defines this charming mountain town.

Browse world-class art pieces inside the Turchin Center for the Visual Arts at Appalachian State University. This celebrated center showcases a stunning blend of creations by national and international artists, establishing Boone as a significant cultural destination in the North Carolina mountains.

activities.text: Experience Boone's thriving craft beverage scene, where local breweries showcase the art of creating refreshing craft beers. Touring the production facilities offers an opportunity to witness the brewing process firsthand and then taste the results, providing a unique conclusion to your exploration of this mountain community.

places.name: Boston, MA

visits.text: In Boston, the story of American independence is quite literally walked—a 2.5-mile red line painted on the sidewalk connects 16 Revolutionary War sites from Boston Common (the oldest public park in the United States, established 1634) to Charlestown. The Massachusetts State House opens the trail: its dome covered in genuine 24-karat gold cost $8 million during its 1997 restoration. Architect Charles Bulfinch designed it in 1798. Free audio guide available at freedomtrail.org, or join the costumed Freedom Trail Players for $15, 90 minutes, and a level of detail you won't find on the plaques.

At Granary Burying Ground (1660), the Puritan gravestones are carved with winged death's heads—a funerary style unique to North America that bears no resemblance to European cemetery traditions. Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, John Hancock, and the five victims of the Boston Massacre rest here. The neighboring King's Chapel Burying Ground (1630) is even older: Mary Chilton, the first woman from the Mayflower to step ashore at Plymouth in 1620, is buried here. Thirty minutes in each is sufficient, though you'll likely linger longer.

In front of the Old State House (1713), look for the plaque on the ground—it marks the exact spot of the Boston Massacre on March 5, 1770, five deaths that triggered the Revolution. The Declaration of Independence was read publicly from this building's balcony on July 18, 1776, and the reenactment takes place every Fourth of July. Faneuil Hall (1742), further along, is where Samuel Adams climbed onto tables to convince his fellow citizens to break with the Crown.

Two sites close the Trail. The Paul Revere House (circa 1680, ticket $6) is the oldest residential home in downtown Boston—Paul Revere lived here when he made his midnight ride on April 18, 1775, to warn the Minutemen. The Old North Church, whose steeple displayed the two lanterns signaling "One if by land, two if by sea," is a 5-minute walk away. Push on to Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown: a 221-foot granite obelisk on the site of the first major battle, fought June 17, 1775.

Acorn Street in Beacon Hill is Boston's most photographed street—uneven cobblestones, gas lamps, packed facades in two tight rows. Fifteen minutes is enough to understand why. Just next door, the Boston Public Garden (1837), America's first public botanical garden, rewards lingering: look for the "Make Way for Ducklings" statue, a tribute to Robert McCloskey's 1941 book that remains, for generations of Americans, their first memory of Boston.

Harvard Yard is home to what students call the "Statue of Three Lies": the inscription reads "John Harvard, Founder, 1638"—but John Harvard was not the founder (merely a major donor), the university dates from 1636 not 1638, and the face sculpted in 1884 by Daniel Chester French is that of an anonymous student, as no portrait of John Harvard survived. Students touch the statue's left foot for exam luck, which has polished it down to bare metal. An additional unofficial tradition surrounds this foot that guides mention with an embarrassed smile.

At the Harvard Museum of Natural History (ticket $15), one collection alone justifies admission: the Glass Flowers. Between 1887 and 1936, Czech glassblowers Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka, father and son, created 4,300 botanically accurate specimens in blown glass—veins, stamens, growth stages rendered with scientific precision. You'll find more famous butterfly collections, but nothing in the world resembles this. Ninety minutes.

Mount Auburn Cemetery in Cambridge (1831) inspired New York's Central Park—this is where the idea of a cemetery as public green space first took shape in the United States. Longfellow, Buckminster Fuller, and Winslow Homer are buried here. What's startling: the place is overrun with joggers and picnickers. Locals don't perceive it as a place of mourning. Ninety minutes, at least.

Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890-1937) was born in Providence, lived his entire life there, almost never left, and is buried there. College Hill, on the east bank of the Providence River, appears textually in The Call of Cthulhu, The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and The Dreams in the Witch House—the streets, the 18th-century brick houses on Benefit Street, the cemeteries. Stephen King, Neil Gaiman, and Guillermo del Toro have all named Lovecraft as the primary influence on modern horror fiction. His texts also contain racism and xenophobia that contemporary readers confront with discomfort—Providence didn't grant him a commemorative plaque until 2013. Walking tour map downloadable at lovecraftartsandsciences.com.

The Providence Athenaeum (251 Benefit Street, ticket $5 for non-members) is a private library from 1838 of intact Victorian beauty, still operational. Lovecraft frequented it. Edgar Allan Poe had visited before him between 1845 and 1849, when he came courting Sarah Helen Whitman—who inspired his poem Annabel Lee. Open to the public certain hours, allow 30 minutes.

Lovecraft's grave at Swan Point Cemetery (585 Blackstone Boulevard) isn't easy to find without a map. From the main entrance: straight ahead to the Barnaby monument, left on Junction Avenue, right on Pond Avenue, T-intersection with Avenue B—the Phillips family plot is ahead, large central obelisk, Lovecraft's stone is small, behind, to the right. Inscription: "I Am Providence." The grave is regularly covered with pens, Cthulhu drawings, plastic octopi, and letters—from fans who come from around the world for this.

activities.text: The North End, the neighborhood around Paul Revere House, is unanimously recognized as the best place for Italian food in the United States. Mamma Maria (3 North Square, $60-100) occupies an 18th-century townhouse, or try Pizzeria Regina for Boston's oldest pizzeria since 1926. Mandatory stop at Mike's Pastry (300 Hanover Street) for cannoli—the line is permanent, $5-8, and worth the wait.

Boston is one of the few places in the United States where gas streetlights still operate—Beacon Hill has dozens, maintained by the city. The cobblestone streets, 18th-century brick rowhouses, Louisburg Square with its $5-15 million homes: an evening in the neighborhood is enough to understand why Bostonians never leave.

The Cheers Bar at 84 Beacon Street is the bar that inspired the 1982 series. Packed with tourists, burger $18-25—but if the show shaped your childhood, spending an hour here is less tourism than personal pilgrimage.

Cambridge is entirely accessible by T from downtown (Red Line, 15 minutes). Massachusetts Avenue between Harvard Square and Porter Square concentrates the independent cafés and specialty bookstores that Bostonians actually frequent. In the evening, Quincy Market since 1826 offers dozens of food stalls for $15-30—the least stuffy spot of the entire week.

Olneyville New York System (18 Plainfield Street) is a Providence institution since 1946: the "wieners" (hot dogs with meat sauce, 3 for $7) were featured by Anthony Bourdain on Parts Unknown. This is Providence's version of authentic local experience. Fancier alternative: Al Forno (577 South Main Street), which invented grilled pizza in 1980 and charges $50-90.

Return to Boston Logan via I-95 North, 1h drive. Car return at the airport—all major agencies on-site. Total car rental budget for the trip: $600-800 for 8 days automatic sedan. Smartphone GPS required.

visits.text: Stroll Pearl Street Mall, pedestrianized since 1977: four blocks of red brick lined with independent shops, cafes, and award-winning restaurants, with the Flatirons as a backdrop. More than 70% of the businesses are local. Food & Wine ranked it among the ten best food streets in America.

The Flatirons—five slabs of sandstone tilted more than 1,000 feet above the city—are impossible to miss. Chautauqua Park, at their base, gives access to about twenty trails. The First Flatiron Trail (2 miles round-trip) offers a bird's-eye view of the city—start at dawn to beat the crowds.

Wander the University of Colorado Boulder campus, founded in 1876—its red sandstone buildings and red-tiled roofs make it one of the most beautiful campuses in the country. A stroll through the University Mall is enough to grasp the atmosphere of this town at 5,430 feet that has made the outdoors its identity.

activities.text: If you're here on a Saturday morning from May to October, don't miss the Boulder Farmers Market: local producers, food trucks, and artisans at the corner of 13th and Canyon Blvd. It's where the community gathers—ideal for assembling a picnic before the Flatirons.

Boulder has several taprooms steps from Pearl Street. Avery Brewing and Twisted Pine are the local references—order a pint on the patio with the Flatirons in the background. It's the end-of-day ritual for locals, and you'll understand why this town is so appealing.

days_plan.itin_title: Colorado-Wyoming Road Trip: National Parks, Rockies & Wide Open Spaces

visits.text: Whitaker Point (Hawksbill Crag) - Arkansas's Most Photographed Natural Wonder: This dramatic rock outcropping extends over a 100-foot drop into the Ozark wilderness, featured in Disney films and gracing countless magazine covers. The 3-mile round-trip hike rewards with vertigo-inducing views across miles of unbroken forest stretching to the horizon.

Roark Bluff - Where Twin Waterfalls Plunge into Paradise: Two spectacular cascades-Roark Bluff Falls and V-Notch Falls-thunder over 100-foot limestone cliffs into the Buffalo River below. Access by canoe or kayak transforms the journey into adventure.

Buffalo National River - America's First National River: Flowing 150 miles through the Ozarks, this pristine waterway remains wild and free, protected since 1972. Towering 500-foot bluffs, hidden caves, and abundant wildlife make every bend a discovery.

activities.text: Buffalo River Float Trip - Paddle Through Living Geology: Multi-day canoe and kayak journeys pass beneath massive bluffs, through swimming holes, and past riverside campsites where elk now roam the restored bottomlands.

Lost Valley & Eden Falls Cave - Underground Waterfall Wonder: A short trail leads to a natural rock shelter harboring a waterfall that disappears into a cave system. The adventurous can scramble inside to witness Eden Falls plunging into complete darkness.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Itinerary: Hot Springs, Ozarks and Natural Parks

visits.text: Butte Historic District — Explore this former copper mining capital where 100 kilometers of underground tunnels honeycomb the hill beneath Victorian mansions and miners' cottages. The National Historic Landmark preserves boom-era architecture from when Butte was the richest hill on Earth.
Berkeley Pit — View this massive open-pit copper mine now filled with toxic acidic water. The 540-meter-deep pit operated 1955-1982 and demonstrates environmental impacts of hardrock mining.

Museum of the Rockies — Discover Montana's natural history including the world's largest Tyrannosaurus rex skull collection. Jack Horner's dinosaur research center houses fossils from Montana's Hell Creek Formation.
Montana State University — Visit this land-grant university founded in 1893 featuring brick buildings and mountain-framed campus. The Gallatin Valley institution enrolls 16,000 students.

activities.text: Bozeman Main Street — Browse outdoor recreation shops, galleries, and restaurants in this thriving mountain town. Bozeman balances Old West heritage with modern amenities serving recreationists.
Brewery and distillery tasting — Sample craft beers and spirits using Montana grains and glacial water. Bozeman's beverage scene reflects the state's agricultural bounty.
Gallatin Valley sunset — Watch alpenglow paint the surrounding peaks pink and orange. The valley's mountain rim creates spectacular evening light displays.

days_plan.itin_title: Montana's Wild Landscapes: Glacier National Park to Yellowstone Geysers

places.name: Branson, MO

visits.text: Silver Dollar City isn't your typical theme park. Beneath its 100 wooded acres lies Marvel Cave, a natural cavern known to the Osage for generations and commercially operated as early as 1894. The park opened in 1960 around it, designed as an 1880s mining town. A hundred resident craftspeople work in public—glassblowers, blacksmiths, potters. The roller coasters are serious business: Outlaw Run is a wooden coaster with an 81-degree drop that set a world record when it opened in 2013. Plan a full day.

The Titanic Museum is a half-scale replica of the ocean liner planted right in the middle of Highway 76—you can't miss it. More than 400 authentic artifacts from the 1912 sinking are on display, including recreated first- and third-class cabins. At the entrance, you receive a boarding pass for an actual passenger. You find out at the end whether they survived.

Branson Landing runs along Lake Taneycomo in the heart of downtown—shops, restaurants, and a choreographed water-and-fire show every hour in the evenings. This is where tourists gather after the shows to walk along the waterfront. Not much happening in the morning, much better after 8 PM with the lake lights.

Table Rock State Park stretches 5 miles southwest of Branson, on the north shore of the lake. This is Branson before the shows: wooded trails along limestone bluffs, white-tailed deer at dawn, kingfishers on the rocks. The marina rents boats and marks diving spots on wrecks deliberately sunk to create artificial reefs. Go before 9 AM—you'll have the trails to yourself.

The Shepherd of the Hills Historic Homestead is the original farm described in Harold Bell Wright's 1907 novel—the book that triggered tourism in the Ozarks and the first American bestseller to exceed one million copies. Old Matt's Cabin still stands. The 230-foot observation tower provides the only 360-degree panorama of the surrounding hills.

The Branson Scenic Railway departs from the historic 1905 depot right downtown. Eighty minutes through the White River Valley gorges, tunnels, steel bridges, and sharp turns along the hillside. This is genuine vintage rolling stock. Take a window seat on the right as you depart—the river views are on that side.

activities.text: Table Rock Lake was created in 1958 by a dam on the White River—76 square miles with 857 miles of shoreline. Book a spot on the Showboat Branson Belle, a paddle-wheel steamboat launched in 1994: to lubricate its launch into the water, engineers used two tons of bananas. The 2-hour cruise includes a three-course meal and a variety show. Unapologetically kitschy, but genuinely enjoyable.

Branson counts dozens of dinner shows along Highway 76—country, gospel, comedy, magic. If you only do one, choose the Shepherd of the Hills Outdoor Drama over the generic shows: performed outdoors since 1960 in an amphitheater facing the hills, it tells Harold Bell Wright's 1907 novel—the book that put the Ozarks on the American tourist map, the first American bestseller to exceed one million copies sold.

Rent a boat on Table Rock Lake for the morning—powerboats, jet skis, and kayaks available at the marinas. On weekdays in the off-season, the rocky coves along the east shore are quiet and the water is clear enough for swimming. Largemouth bass fishing is good on this lake—ask the rental operator which areas are open for the day.

If you're traveling with kids, Fritz's Adventure is Branson's second-biggest attraction after Silver Dollar City. Seven stories of zip lines, climbing walls, and tunnels in a 50,000-square-foot building, opened in 2014. Without kids, skip it—but if you have them, it's two hours of peace for you.

visits.text: Ascend Brasstown Bald, Georgia's highest peak at 4,784 feet, where an observation tower provides 360-degree panoramas across four states on clear days. The summit trail climbs through misty forests draped in wildflowers during spring and brilliant foliage in autumn, rewarding hikers with some of the most spectacular mountain views in the American Southeast. Interpretive exhibits at the visitor center explain the region's ecology and Cherokee heritage.

Explore the broader Northeast Georgia Mountains region, a landscape of forested ridges, cascading waterfalls, and crystal-clear streams that has attracted nature lovers for generations. Scenic byways wind through quaint mountain communities where local artisans create traditional crafts and family-owned vineyards produce award-winning wines. The area offers world-class hiking, fishing, and wildlife observation.

activities.text: Visit Château Élan winery for tastings of Georgia wines accompanied by vineyard tours explaining traditional winemaking techniques. The rolling hills, elegant tasting rooms, and relaxing atmosphere make this an ideal introduction to the state's emerging wine region.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia's Grand Circle: Caucasus Mountains, Tbilisi & Black Sea Coast

places.name: Breaux Bridge, LA

visits.text: Leave Baton Rouge via I-10 heading west. After 40 minutes, you'll cross the Atchafalaya Basin on an 18-mile elevated highway bridge over America's largest swamp—the view is striking, especially in the morning when mist floats above the cypress trees. Exit at Henderson (exit 115) for a bayou boat tour. Local operators offer 90-minute to 2-hour tours through the basin's channels: you'll see alligators, great blue herons, egrets, and turtles in a landscape of bald cypress draped with Spanish moss.

After the bayou, drive 15 minutes to Breaux Bridge, nicknamed "Crawfish Capital of the World" by Louisiana's legislature since 1959. The small downtown on the banks of Bayou Teche has authentic Cajun charm: painted wooden houses, art galleries, music shops, and restaurants that smell of roux and cayenne. Walk across the bridge spanning the bayou—the first bridge here was built in 1799 by Acadian pioneer Firmin Breaux.

activities.text: Make a detour to Lake Martin, between Breaux Bridge and Lafayette (10 minutes). This nature preserve harbors a colony of herons, egrets, and ibis—during nesting season (March-June), the trees are literally covered with white birds. You can drive along the lake on Rookery Road or rent a kayak to weave between the cypress trees. Alligators are common—keep your distance.

Evening in Breaux Bridge, look for a restaurant with live Cajun music. On Saturday mornings, several venues offer a "zydeco breakfast"—breakfast accompanied by live zydeco music, with people getting up to dance between tables. If you're here on a weekday, inquire about evening "Cajun jams."

visits.text: Drive the final 5 kilometers to Bodie State Historic Park (38.2125, -119.0119) on unpaved road—slow, rough, 15-20 minutes from CA-270. No gas, no food, no water on site: fill up in Bridgeport beforehand. Arriving at the parking lot, 110 gray wooden buildings spread across the hills, silent, beneath the Sierra Nevada sky. The park's policy is called "arrested decay": nothing is restored, but nothing collapses. Interiors are left exactly as the last inhabitants left them in the 1940s-1960s—dishes on tables, tools on workbenches, books open on shelves, toys on floors in family homes. Ticket $8.

In 1879, Bodie had 8,000 to 10,000 residents, 65 saloons, several brothels, 200 restaurants, a bowling alley, and daily newspapers. The town was known as the most violent in the West—a gunfight a day, a murder a week on average. An 8-year-old girl whose family was moving here scribbled in her diary: "Goodbye God, I'm going to Bodie." The phrase became a proverb throughout the American West. Visit the schoolhouse (38.2128, -119.0144)—written blackboards, desks, open books, inkwells, as if class had just been interrupted—and Bodie Bank (38.2114, -119.0156) whose safe, a blackened metal cube, is the only object that survived the 1932 fire.

Finish at Bodie Cemetery (38.2150, -119.0172)—19th-century graves with names of documented violent deaths, and the adjacent Boot Hill where the "unworthy" were buried: prostitutes, criminals, suicides, and Chinese in the same common grave. The Chinese community ran the laundries and supplied the town with wood from a Chinatown northwest of Main Street—discrimination in the mines, but indispensable outside them. The Standard Mill (38.2128, -119.0169) offers guided tours on weekends at 1 PM ($6 additional, excellent quality).

activities.text: Bring a picnic—there's nothing to eat in Bodie or within a 30-kilometer radius. Get it in Bridgeport before leaving in the morning. Allow 4-5 hours on site total: the self-guided tour brochure ($3) at the visitor center ensures you don't miss anything.

Return to Bridgeport (38.2557, -119.2298) for the night—motels and B&Bs, $90-180/night. A small, unpretentious mountain town, but Bodie can't be visited in the evening (closes at 6 PM in summer, 3 PM in winter). Rainbow Bar & Grill on Main Street is the local spot for simple dinner after the day.

days_plan.itin_title: 10-Day American Far West: San Francisco, Yosemite, Bodie Ghost Town, Death Valley, Las Vegas & Grand Canyon

visits.text: Day 1 - End the day on the Brooklyn Bridge: 1883 steel cables and wooden promenade above the traffic. Start on the Manhattan side and walk at least to the first tower, the view over the harbor at sunset rewards the day. Count 30 to 45 min round trip, dense crowds late afternoon.

Day 1 - The Brooklyn Bridge pedestrian path is now bike-free, with cyclists relegated to the roadway: you can advance better than before. The neo-Gothic arches frame the skyline; the best photos happen early morning or at blue hour. Tripod unnecessary, the structure vibrates with passing subway and cars.

activities.text: If legs hold up, cross entirely and descend on the Brooklyn side to dine in Dumbo facing Manhattan's lights, before returning by subway.
End-of-day option: head to the Whitehall terminal, at Manhattan's southern tip, for the Staten Island ferry. Subway from Brooklyn Bridge, about 9.5 km, 40 to 45 min with transfer.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Day 5 - Suspended above the expressway, the Brooklyn Heights Promenade unfurls the classic panorama over Lower Manhattan, the bridges, and the statue in the distance. Benches, old trees, residential calm: locals walk their dogs facing the skyline. Free, any hour; sunset is superb there.

Day 5 - Behind the promenade, Brooklyn Heights lines up its 1840s brownstones on fruit-named streets: Cranberry, Pineapple, Orange Street. Truman Capote wrote here. Ten minutes' detour through Willow Street gives the movie America you came for.

activities.text: Artisanal ice cream at the bridge foot, to enjoy along the promenade: the quintessential Brooklyn combo.
Subway to Brooklyn Museum: 4 km, 2/3 lines from Clark Street or Borough Hall to Eastern Parkway-Brooklyn Museum, about 25 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Day 5 - The Brooklyn Museum, often eclipsed by its Manhattan cousins, houses one of the city's richest collections: remarkable ancient Egypt, Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party, sharp pop exhibitions. Nonexistent lines compared to the Met. Count 2 hours; first Saturday of the month, free festive evening.

Day 5 - Adjacent to the museum, the Brooklyn Botanic Garden is worth the combined ticket in spring: the cherry esplanade in bloom, late April, is an event unto itself, Japanese garden in support. For lack of time, simply choose: the garden in good weather, the museum in rain.

activities.text: Possible detour through Prospect Park, designed by Central Park's creators, which many Brooklynites judge more successful than the original.
Subway to Green-Wood Cemetery: 3 km, about 20 min, 25th Street station (R line) drops at the main entrance foot.

places.name: Brooks Camp, AK

visits.text: Brooks Falls is a 6-foot drop on the Brooks River—nothing spectacular in itself. What is spectacular is that dozens of brown bears, some exceeding 900 pounds, position themselves here to catch sockeye salmon returning to spawn. The NPS viewing platforms, equipped with ramps and waiting areas, are limited to 40 people at a time with hourly rotation in July. In peak season, expect 90-minute waits—come at 5 a.m. or after 7 p.m. to avoid crowds.

The Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes—accessible from Brooks Camp via the park's only vehicle road (16 miles of dirt track)—is the result of the 1912 eruption of Novarupta volcano, the largest of the 20th century worldwide. Millions of tons of ash blanketed the valley across 75 miles. Today the landscape resembles the surface of the Moon: dotted with fumaroles, valleys carved into pumice rock, utterly devoid of vegetation. The park bus makes the round trip from Brooks Camp.

The Katmai Visitor Center at Brooks Camp—modest but well-designed—traces the park's volcanic history and its designation as a national monument in 1918, long before bears made it famous. The daily ranger talks (free) are often among the best you'll hear in the entire U.S. national park system.

The Riffles Platform—the second viewing platform, downstream from Brooks Falls—is often overlooked in favor of the falls. That's a mistake: dominant bears that can't secure a spot at the falls fish here in the shallows, often just yards from the platform. The atmosphere is different, more intimate, and there's almost no wait.

The shore of Naknek Lake from Brooks Camp is a discreet but effective observation post to watch bears stroll the beach, especially late in the day. Naknek Lake is the park's largest (about 242 square miles) and feeds the Brooks River where salmon concentrate. Settle on the rocks in the evening with binoculars—don't attempt to go down to the beach if bears are present.

activities.text: The Brooks River has been a world-class fishing river since the 1950s. Rainbow trout, king salmon, and sockeye salmon can be caught with light flies from the banks, in waders. There's one absolute rule: if a bear approaches your spot, you leave—no discussion. Rangers on-site review the protocols upon arrival. Licenses available at the lodge.

The Dumpling Mountain trail (4.5 miles round-trip, 1,500 feet of elevation gain) starts at Brooks Camp and climbs above treeline to panoramic views over Naknek Lake, the Alaska Peninsula mountains, and on clear days, all the way to the Pacific. Go early in the morning—bears are active on the slopes in the evening.

Kayaking on Naknek Lake from Brooks Camp—kayaks are available for rent through Katmailand. On the water, you're at the same level as bears on shore, at a safe distance. Early morning, the lake is often mirror-flat and the reflection of the volcanoes breathtaking. Avoid outings after 6 p.m.—wind picks up quickly.

Katmai's Fat Bear Week is an internet phenomenon that drew over 800,000 votes in 2021—but before voting online, come observe in real life. In September, bears that spent the summer fishing accumulate fat reserves at an astonishing rate. Some individuals, like the famous Bear 747, can weigh over 1,400 pounds by the start of winter. Rangers at Brooks Camp know the names and histories of every regular bear—ask them.

visits.text: Discover Brunswick, the historic mainland gateway to the Golden Isles, where Victorian architecture, tree-lined streets, and scenic tidal rivers create understated coastal charm. The centuries-old Lover's Oak, a massive live oak beneath which couples have traditionally pledged their devotion, spreads its ancient branches over a peaceful park. The Old Town district preserves authentic small-town Georgia character.

Tour Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation, a remarkably intact antebellum rice plantation documenting the complex history of agriculture, slavery, and Southern society along Georgia's tidal rivers. The quiet marina and working waterfront reflect Brunswick's enduring connection to the sea. Cross the stunning Sidney Lanier Bridge for spectacular views of the coastal landscape.

activities.text: Sample locally crafted spirits at Georgia's only rum distillery, where small-batch production creates distinctive rums with notes of dark cherry and caramel. The mainland location provides convenient access to all the Golden Isles while offering more affordable accommodations than the islands themselves.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia's Grand Circle: Caucasus Mountains, Tbilisi & Black Sea Coast

visits.text: Day 3 - Bryant Park, a lawn set between towers, serves as Midtown's open-air cafeteria: movable chairs, kiosks, pétanque and ping-pong. In winter, free ice rink (skate rental paid) and holiday market. It's Day 3's natural lunch break, midway through the day.

Day 3 - Backing the park, the New York Public Library guards the entrance with its two marble lions, Patience and Fortitude. Climb to the Rose Main Reading Room, 295-foot reading hall with painted ceiling: free access, silence required. The setting served Ghostbusters as well as The Day After Tomorrow.

activities.text: Sandwich or salad to go, green chair in the sun: the most New York lunch there is, for under $15.
Walk to Times Square: 500 m via 42nd Street or Broadway, about 6 min.

visits.text: Bryce Amphitheater - Bryce Canyon isn't technically a canyon but rather a collection of amphitheaters carved into the Paunsaugunt Plateau. The rocks, deposited at the bottom of an ancient lake 55 million years ago, get their colors from oxidized iron and manganese. Start at Sunrise Point for the overview: thousands of orange, pink, and cream-colored hoodoos rise like a petrified army. This is where the Queen's Garden trail begins.

Sunset Point - Half a mile from Sunrise Point via the Rim Trail, this is the starting point for the Navajo Loop. From the rim, you'll spot Thor's Hammer, a 30-foot hoodoo topped by a precariously balanced caprock that defies gravity. The plunging view into Wall Street, a slot canyon lined with Douglas firs, is vertigo-inducing.

Continue to Inspiration Point and Bryce Point for even broader amphitheater panoramas. Bryce Point, at the end of the road, offers the most spectacular perspective - you take in the entire amphitheater in a single sweeping view.

activities.text: Queen's Garden - Navajo Loop - The must-do hike at Bryce. Descend via Queen's Garden from Sunrise Point (the gentlest descent), walk among the hoodoos past the Queen Victoria formation - a pinnacle that resembles a crowned queen - then climb back up via the Navajo Loop and its tight switchbacks between the towering walls of Wall Street. The loop is 3 miles with 650 feet of elevation change; allow 1.5 to 2 hours. The park sits at 8,000 feet elevation: take your time, the air is thinner than it feels.

If you're here between April and October, stay for sunset from Sunset Point - the hoodoos shift from orange to deep crimson in minutes. The park is also certified Dark Sky: on clear nights, the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye. Bring a warm layer; it can get chilly at this elevation even in summer.

places.name: Buffalo, NY

visits.text: Frank Lloyd Wright's Darwin Martin House — Tour this Prairie School masterpiece completed in 1905, considered Wright's most important work before Fallingwater. The complex features 394 art glass windows and doors creating geometric light patterns throughout interconnected spaces.

Albright-Knox Art Gallery — Explore this museum renowned for its contemporary and modern art collection spanning Impressionism to Pop Art. The 1905 Greek Revival building houses works by Picasso, Matisse, Pollock, and Warhol.

Buffalo City Hall — Ascend to the 28th-floor observation deck of this 1931 Art Deco skyscraper for panoramic city and lake views. The 115-meter tower features intricate Native American motifs and Art Deco ornamentation throughout its limestone facade.

Canalside — Stroll along Buffalo's revitalized waterfront where the Erie Canal met Lake Erie beginning in 1825. The harbor development features historic naval vessels, kayak launches, and winter ice skating on refrigerated outdoor rinks.

activities.text: Buffalo wings at Anchor Bar — Taste the original Buffalo wing invented here accidentally in 1964 by Teressa Bellissimo. The deep-fried chicken wings tossed in cayenne pepper hot sauce and served with celery and blue cheese became a global phenomenon.

Elmwood Village neighborhood walk — Browse boutiques, galleries, and cafes in this vibrant historic district listed on the National Register. Tree-lined streets showcase Victorian and Colonial Revival architecture from Buffalo's Gilded Age prosperity.

Sunset at Times Beach Nature Preserve — Observe migrating birds and watch sailboats on the Niagara River at this 37-hectare urban wilderness. The preserve's wetlands and meadows attract over 200 bird species along the Atlantic Flyway.

places.name: Burlington, VT

visits.text: Church Street Marketplace makes itself known the moment you set foot in Burlington: a four-block pedestrian street voted best public space in the United States by USA Today in 2022, with over 100 shops and restaurants and street musicians on every corner. The ECHO Leahy Center for Lake Champlain, on the waterfront, is an interactive museum featuring the lake's 81 fish species—worth seeing if you're traveling with children.

Waterfront Park opens onto Lake Champlain with New York's Adirondacks as backdrop—settle on the boardwalk at sunset. Named by Samuel de Champlain in 1609, the lake stretches for 120 miles and contains 6.8 trillion gallons of water. The Burlington Bike Path follows 7.5 miles of shoreline and joins the Island Line Trail, a converted railway running for miles above the lake's waters.

If you're here on a Saturday morning, the Burlington Farmers Market takes over City Hall Park: local producers, artisan bakeries, cheesemakers, and maple syrup cabins side by side. Taste a creemee—the local maple soft serve—before hitting the road toward Providence.

activities.text: Burlington is regularly ranked among the cities with the highest density of breweries per capita in the United States—try Foam Brewers on the waterfront, Zero Gravity, or Switchback Brewing Company. In the evening, the Spirit of Ethan Allen offers dinner cruises on the lake with views of the Adirondacks at sunset.

Six miles south, the Shelburne Museum is one of the most comprehensive collections of Americana in the country: 150,000 objects distributed across 39 historic buildings including a steamboat that once sailed Lake Champlain. Budget 3 hours minimum—open May through November, admission ~$30.

visits.text: Leave Los Angeles via the Pacific Coast Highway heading north. The first Malibu beaches begin 19 miles from downtown—this is where movie stars' homes have clustered since the 1920s. Stop at Zuma Beach for a break before continuing to Santa Barbara.

Santa Barbara calls itself the 'American Riviera.' Mission Santa Barbara, founded in 1786, is one of California's 21 Franciscan missions and one of the few never abandoned since its founding. The neoclassical facade you see today dates from 1833. Stearns Wharf, California's oldest working pier built in 1872, extends 2,100 feet into the sea—ideal for spotting dolphins and seals.

activities.text: Arrive in Cambria by late afternoon. This small village of 6,000 residents is wedged between wooded hills and Pacific cliffs. Moonstone Beach is scattered with translucent pebbles—the moonstones that gave the beach its name. Dine facing the ocean.

visits.text: Scout the Goonies locations in Astoria—the sets from Richard Donner's 1985 film are almost all still there. Drive up to 368 38th Street to see Mikey's house (46.1898, -123.8405): Victorian on the hill, private property, residents have nailed a "No Trespassing" sign because they've had enough. Photo from the sidewalk, gate closed. Astoria High School (46.1898, -123.8264) served as the high school in classroom scenes, still in operation. The Oregon Film Museum (46.1894, -123.8284), 732 Duane Street, is housed in the old jail used for the Fratelli escape sequence—ticket $6, 30 minutes, with sections dedicated to other Oregon shoots (Free Willy, Stand By Me, Kindergarten Cop, Twilight).

Climb to the Astoria Column (46.1801, -123.8232), 1 Coxcomb Drive—125-foot tower built in 1926, spiral frieze retracing the region's history, views over the Columbia and estuary. Buy a $1 balsa glider at the tower's base and launch it from the top: local tradition since the 1980s, the gliders spiral for a long time before getting lost in the trees. Parking $5.

Drive 5 minutes south of Astoria to Lewis and Clark National Historical Park (46.1342, -123.8772) to see Fort Clatsop—wooden replica of the fort where Lewis and Clark spent winter 1805-1806 at the end of 4,200 miles from Missouri. It rained 95 days out of the 106 they spent there, exactly the kind of conditions that still prevail here in November. 20-minute film included, ticket $7.

Haystack Rock (45.8851, -123.9686) at Cannon Beach commands attention before you've even left the car—235 feet of black basalt emerging 300 feet from shore, a nature reserve where tufted puffins nest from April to July. This is where the final Goonies scene takes place, One-Eyed Willy's ship offshore. The photo is the one you'll find twenty years from now remembering the trip.

activities.text: Bowl a game at Lower Columbia Bowl (46.1881, -123.8298), 826 Marine Drive—the bowling alley where Chunk does his "Truffle Shuffle" in Goonies, still operating and open to the public. $15-20 per person, more authentic than a plastic souvenir.

Drive down US-101 to Cannon Beach (35 minutes south) for the night. Dine facing the ocean on Hemlock Street, seafood, $35-65. Book a beachside hotel with Haystack Rock views if you're coming in season—$180-380, and sunrise from the room is worth the price.

visits.text: Hike the Skinny Dip Falls Trailhead, where scenic forest trails lead through beautiful Appalachian woodland to a stunning waterfall and refreshing swimming spot. This natural treasure offers the perfect escape into the wilderness that surrounds this charming Haywood County town near Asheville.

Explore Graveyard Fields, a unique high-altitude area offering mysterious and captivating views of the Blue Ridge Mountains. This popular hiking destination features unusual landscapes and abundant wildflowers, providing outdoor enthusiasts with unforgettable mountain experiences.

activities.text: Discover local artistry at Cold Mountain Art Collective, where regional artists showcase their creative works inspired by the surrounding mountain landscape. Browse handcrafted items at Willow Hill Soap Company, known for their artistic and decorative candles that make perfect souvenirs of your mountain adventure.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: From Outer Banks Beaches to Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Kennedy Space Center - Where Humans Reach for the Stars: This historic launch complex has sent every American astronaut into orbit since the 1960s. The visitor complex offers encounters with real astronauts, full-scale rocket displays, and the actual Space Shuttle Atlantis.

Rocket Garden - Walk Among Giants: Stand beneath authentic rockets from every era of American spaceflight, from Mercury through Apollo, experiencing the scale of humanity's greatest engineering achievements.

Canaveral National Seashore - 24 Miles of Undeveloped Atlantic Coast: NASA's need for privacy created this unintended benefit-a pristine refuge protecting sea turtle nesting beaches and 1,000+ plant species.

activities.text: Rocket Launch Viewing - Watch History Being Made: Multiple companies now launch from Cape Canaveral, with public viewing areas offering front-row seats to thundering liftoffs that shake the ground miles away.

IMAX Theater and 4D Experience - Space Exploration Immersion: State-of-the-art theaters present the wonders of space exploration through footage shot by astronauts aboard the International Space Station.

days_plan.itin_title: The Ultimate Florida Keys Road Trip: From Miami to Key West

visits.text: Provincetown is worth the two-hour drive from the Cape's entrance—don't skip it. The Pilgrim Monument (1910) recalls that the Pilgrims anchored the Mayflower here in November 1620, before Plymouth, and drafted the Mayflower Compact. The 252-foot granite tower is the tallest all-granite structure in the United States. A mile away, Race Point Beach spreads its 100-foot dunes facing the open Atlantic.

Chatham delivers the postcard Cape Cod image: Main Street lines up shops, art galleries, and seafood restaurants in white clapboard buildings. Chatham Fish Pier comes alive early morning when the boats arrive—you can buy fresh tuna directly from the fishermen. Chatham Lighthouse (1878) overlooks the beach from atop a bluff.

Cape Cod National Seashore has protected 50 square miles of coastline since 1961: Atlantic beaches, dunes, pine forests, and salt marshes. Enter through the Salt Pond Visitor Center in Eastham for a trail map. Coast Guard Beach and Nauset Light Beach are the Cape's wildest beaches—cool water, few people on weekdays.

The moment the ferry docks in Oak Bluffs, head to Trinity Park: over 300 painted wooden cottages in vivid colors form a unique ensemble, the "Gingerbread Houses" built from the 1860s onward on the site of a Methodist camp meeting. The central cast-iron Tabernacle (1879) still hosts summer concerts. Circuit Avenue, the main street, is lined with shops and restaurants.

Edgartown, founded in 1642, is the island's historic center. The 19th-century whaling captains' houses line their white facades along Water Street—stop at the Martha's Vineyard Historical Society, at the Cooke House (1765), which preserves documents and objects related to the whaling era. A 3-minute ferry crosses the channel to Chappaquiddick Island.

At the island's western tip, the Gay Head Cliffs of Aquinnah rise 200 feet above the Atlantic. Step to the edge to watch the clay change color with the light—ochre, red, white, gray. These lands belong to the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), which regained them in 1987. The Gay Head Lighthouse (1844) is reachable on foot from the parking lot. Caution: erosion is rapid.

activities.text: Embark on a whale watching trip from MacMillan Pier in Provincetown: 3-4 hour excursions to Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary, 5 miles north of the Cape, allow you to observe humpback whales, finbacks, and dolphins. The Dolphin Fleet offers daily departures May through October—book online, ~$50 per person. Morning trips have the best sea conditions.

The Cape Cod Rail Trail winds for 25 miles along a 19th-century railway bed—rent a bike and go: the path crosses dunes, glacial ponds, and scrub oak forests. Rental points dot the route. It's the most pleasant way to cross the Cape without a car.

Rent a bike at the ferry exit in Oak Bluffs and ride the island via State Road to Aquinnah (14 miles): the route crosses oak forests, meadows, and skirts Tisbury Pond. Martha's Vineyard is flat and the bike network well developed—count on ~$30 per day.

In the evening, go eat in Menemsha, the small fishing port on the west side of the island. The lobster is caught that very morning and cooked to order—eat on the docks watching the boats come in and the sun set over Vineyard Sound.

Boston, Maine & the Islands: 10 Days Through New England

visits.text: Explore Capulin Volcano National Monument, where an extinct cinder cone volcano rises dramatically from the surrounding plains, providing a remarkable example of geologically recent volcanic activity in the American Southwest. The paved road spirals to the crater rim, where hiking trails circle the edge and descend into the volcanic crater itself. From the summit, views extend across four states on clear days, revealing the vast grassland plains that characterize this corner of New Mexico.

activities.text: Watch for diverse wildlife including elk, coyotes, and black bears that inhabit the volcanic slopes and surrounding grasslands. The monument preserves not only geological features but also prairie ecosystems that once supported vast bison herds and continue to shelter numerous species adapted to this high plains environment.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Pueblo Culture, Volcanic Fields and White Sands

visits.text: Descend into Carlsbad Caverns National Park, where more than 100 limestone caves beneath the Chihuahuan Desert reveal spectacular underground formations created over millions of years. The park's namesake Carlsbad Cavern features the famous Big Room, one of the largest cave chambers in North America, where massive stalactites and stalagmites create an otherworldly landscape 750 feet below the surface. Guided tours reveal increasingly remote sections of this subterranean wonderland.

Marvel at Lechuguilla Cave, the nation's deepest limestone cave at 1,567 feet and fourth longest, containing rare mineral formations found nowhere else on Earth. While this cave is closed to general visitors due to its scientific importance, exhibits explain the extraordinary discoveries made within its pristine passages. The park protects over 300 caves beneath the desert surface.

activities.text: Witness the spectacular evening bat flight from May through October, when hundreds of thousands of Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral from the cave entrance at dusk to hunt insects across the desert. Ranger programs explain the ecology of these remarkable creatures and their importance to the cave ecosystem. Drive Walnut Canyon Desert Loop to experience the Chihuahuan Desert landscape above ground.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Pueblo Culture, Volcanic Fields and White Sands

visits.text: Carlsbad Caverns - Descend via the natural entrance: a gaping maw in the rock where a 1.25-mile trail spirals 750 feet underground. The route passes monumental limestone formations before reaching the Big Room, the largest single cave chamber in North America - 357,000 square feet, roughly six football fields. The temperature stays at 56°F year-round, so bring a jacket. If your knees can't handle the descent, an elevator drops you straight into the Big Room.

Carlsbad Museum and Art Center - If you still have energy after the caverns, swing by this small free museum in town. You'll see Permian fossils, Southwestern art, and a collection of Native American pottery.

activities.text: Bat Flight Program - From May through October, between 200,000 and 500,000 Brazilian free-tailed bats emerge from the caverns at dusk to hunt insects. Settle into the stone amphitheater facing the cave entrance. The show begins when a black spiral starts twisting skyward - it lasts 20 to 40 minutes. Rangers give a presentation before the flight. Free, no reservations needed.

days_plan.itin_title: Desert Parks of Texas and New Mexico: Big Bend, Carlsbad, White Sands, and Guadalupe

places.name: Carmel By The Sea, CA

visits.text: Carmel-by-the-Sea - A Storybook Village on the Pacific: This enchanting town has no street addresses, no streetlights, no chain stores, and no high heels allowed on sidewalks without a permit. Fairy-tale cottages with names instead of numbers line streets designed for wandering.

Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo - California's Most Beautiful Mission: Founded in 1770 by Father Junípero Serra, this graceful stone church with its distinctive bell tower served as headquarters for the California mission chain. Serra is buried at the altar.

Carmel Beach - White Sand Without the Crowds: This pristine crescent of powdery white sand, backed by Monterey cypress, consistently ranks among California's most beautiful beaches. Dogs run free and bonfires glow at sunset.

activities.text: Point Lobos State Natural Reserve - The Crown Jewel of the State Park System: Often called 'the greatest meeting of land and water in the world,' this reserve protects 550 acres of headlands, coves, and meadows where sea lions bark and sea otters float in kelp beds.

places.name: Casper, WY

visits.text: Pull off I-25 for the National Historic Trails Interpretive Center - free admission, and one of Wyoming's better history museums. Casper sits at the crossing of four western migration corridors: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, and Pony Express trails. The museum covers the 400,000 emigrants who crossed this ground between 1841 and 1868, with hands-on exhibits including a virtual covered wagon ride and a treadmill that simulates pulling a handcart. A 27-minute film addresses US treaty violations with Plains tribes. Allow 75-90 minutes.

Fort Caspar Museum sits on the banks of the North Platte River in a reconstructed 1865 military post - named for 2nd Lieutenant Caspar Collins, killed at the Battle of Platte Bridge Station that year. A typo in the 1889 town registration swapped the 'a' for an 'e' in Casper, which is why the town and the fort are spelled differently. The museum covers prehistoric Plains Indians, the frontier army, and the energy industry. Open daily May through September.

visits.text: The nickname "Grand Canyon of the East" is a bit presumptuous—but when you're standing on the rim, 180 meters above the Genesee River, you stop arguing. Letchworth State Park was even named the best state park in the United States by USA Today in 2015. The gorge stretches 27 kilometers, the park covers 14,350 acres, and 66 miles of trails wind through it. Three main entrances: Mount Morris to the north, Castile in the center, Portageville to the south. A car is essential to move between them.

This is where William Pryor Letchworth, a Buffalo industrialist, lived from 1859 until his death in 1910, before bequeathing his 1,000-acre estate to the state to become a park. Middle Falls, the widest and tallest of the three main waterfalls at 33 meters, is visible from the esplanade behind the Glen Iris Inn—his house transformed into an inn in 1914. The restaurant still operates; you can have lunch without staying overnight. Direct view of the cascade from the terrace.

Upper Falls, 21 meters high and 90 wide, sits beneath the imposing Portageville railroad viaduct—a 250-meter-long steel arch bridge completed in 2017, replacing the 1875 wooden trestle. Norfolk Southern freight trains still cross several times daily. If you wait a bit, it's worth it for the photo.

Lower Falls, accessible via a 127-step trail descending into the gorge, marks the end of the three-waterfall stretch. Modest height (21 meters) but wilder setting, with a footbridge spanning the river mid-slope. Often deserted compared to the other two, so pleasant in summer.

activities.text: Picnic at Tea Table Overlook, a developed viewing point on the gorge rim in the park's northern section, accessible by car. Stone tables, plunging view of the river 150 meters below. This is the postcard photo spot, and it's free. Self-serve ice cream at the Trading Post at the Castile entrance.

Whitewater rafting with Adventure Calls Outfitters, departing from Mount Morris north of the park. 5 km trip through class II-III rapids depending on season, about 90 minutes on the water, guiding included. Available April through October, more intense in spring after snowmelt. If water doesn't appeal, the same company offers hot air balloons at dawn—Letchworth is one of the few U.S. parks where it's permitted.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Berkshires to Niagara Falls: 10 Days of Waterfalls, Villages & Wilderness

places.name: Cave City, KY

visits.text: Welcome underground. Mammoth Cave is the world's longest known cave system - 426 miles of mapped passages to date, 1.5 times the length of the world's second-longest system. The limestone rock began forming 330 million years ago when Kentucky was still at the bottom of a tropical sea. Native Americans explored these passages 4,000 years ago: their woven moccasins and reed torches have been found several miles from the entrance. Stop at the Visitor Center first to pick up your tickets - the cave stays 54°F year-round, bring a layer even in summer.

Take the Historic Tour first (2 hours, 2 miles, about 540 steps): it's the signature experience. You descend into the Rotunda where enslaved people mined saltpeter for gunpowder during the War of 1812, then pass the tuberculosis huts built in 1842 by Dr. Croghan - who believed underground air would cure his patients. They all died. Gothic Avenue is lined with soot inscriptions left by early visitors as far back as the 19th century. Stephen Bishop, enslaved and then freed guide, mapped much of the system in the 1830s; his grave is visible near the entrance.

In the afternoon, follow up with the Frozen Niagara Tour (1h15, quarter-mile, easy): a different section of the system, visually very different. Here formations dominate - stalactites, stalagmites, and the great cascading rock draperies that look like a petrified waterfall. Two tours in one day are enough to get a complete picture of the system's diversity.

If you want to go deeper, the Violet City Lantern Tour (3 hours, 3 miles) completely changes the atmosphere: rangers turn off all electric lighting and you advance by lantern like in the 19th century. The immensity of the passages becomes palpable when artificial light disappears. It's the favorite tour of several park rangers - and one of the most powerful underground experiences of this road trip.

9 miles north of the park, Lost River Cave in Bowling Green deserves a stop: it's one of the largest cave openings in the eastern United States, with an underground river navigable by boat. The cave served as a nightclub in the 1930s - a sign recalls this improbable period at the entrance. The boat tour lasts 45 minutes.

activities.text: Between tours, enjoy the surface: the Green River Ferry (free, NPS-operated) crosses the river every 10-15 minutes. On the other side, the shaded banks are nearly deserted on weekdays. The First Creek Lake Loop trail (1.5 miles, flat) follows a wet prairie frequented by deer and wild turkeys - a good way to decompress between underground plunges.

In the evening, Cave City a few miles south has decent restaurants and affordable motels. If you prefer sleeping in the park, The Lodge at Mammoth Cave is right on-site - convenient for being there first thing when tours open the next morning.

For thrill-seekers, the Wild Cave Tour (6 hours, 5.5 miles) is the park's most demanding tour: six hours crawling through tight passages, climbing in the dark, and squeezing through sections the standard tours never visit. Bring old clothes - you'll emerge covered in mud. Minimum age 16, reservation required well in advance.

If you prefer staying above ground, the park's 70 miles of trails traverse the karst hills of Kentucky - a landscape of sinkholes, springs, and depressions typical of this limestone terrain. The Sal Hollow Trail (4.5 miles) follows a wooded valley along a creek, nearly empty of people.

places.name: Cedar Rapids, IA

visits.text: You enter a 50,000-square-foot Smithsonian Affiliate on the Cedar River's south bank, which began in 1978 as the Czech Fine Arts Foundation. Its crown jewel is the largest collection of traditional Czech and Slovak kroje (folk costumes) outside the Czech Republic and Slovakia, including pieces dating back to the 16th century. The Immigrant Home exhibit - a surviving 19th-century Bohemian house relocated to higher ground after the devastating 2008 Cedar River flood - walks you through five generations of one family's American story. Admission charged.

Cedar Rapids native Grant Wood painted American Gothic in 1930 in a studio right here in downtown Cedar Rapids. The museum holds the world's largest public collection of Wood's work, from early Impressionist experiments to the regionalist paintings that made him a national figure. The Grant Wood Studio itself is a separate site a few blocks away - advance booking required for studio access. Admission charged.

You drive 30 miles south to Iowa's original state capitol, which housed the legislative assembly from 1842 until 1857, when the seat of government moved west to Des Moines. The building then became the anchor of the University of Iowa campus - a National Historic Landmark standing at the heart of the Pentacrest. The cornerstone was laid in 1840, and the restored period rooms inside represent the building's 1840s-1850s appearance. Free admission; closed Sundays and Mondays.

activities.text: You push open the door to Prairie Lights, founded in 1978 by Jim Harris and moved in 1982 to its current 11,000-square-foot quarters - the same building where Iowa City's literary society met in the 1930s, hosting readings by Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, and Langston Hughes. Seven Nobel Prize laureates in literature have read here, including Toni Morrison and J.M. Coetzee. The Live from Prairie Lights reading series runs four or five nights a week. Check the calendar before your visit.

You wander along 16th Avenue SW through Cedar Rapids' Czech Village, passing the NCSML, where North America's only Orloj - a working replica of Prague's medieval astronomical clock - stands in front of the museum. The adjacent NewBo (New Bohemia) district has converted old industrial buildings into a food market, breweries, and galleries. You can walk both neighborhoods in under an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Iowa and Midwest Road Trip: Great Plains Loop
Iowa and Midwest Road Trip: Great Plains Loop
Iowa Backroads: From the Missouri Bluffs to the Mississippi Cliffs

visits.text: Cedarburg Historic Downtown - Over 200 nineteenth-century buildings line the streets of this small town north of Milwaukee. Old woolen mills converted into shops and galleries at Cedar Creek Settlement, a covered wooden bridge (Wisconsin's last), and cobblestone streets full of charm. This is one of the state's best-preserved downtowns.
Cedarburg Covered Bridge - Built in 1876, this is Wisconsin's last remaining covered bridge. It spans Cedar Creek in a wooded setting north of town.
Cedar Creek Settlement - The former woolen mill (1864) now houses a winery, art galleries, and craft shops. The limestone building is impressive.

activities.text: Craft Breweries and Distilleries - Cedarburg has embraced the craft trend. Several breweries and a distillery offer tastings. This is Wisconsin - beer is serious business here.
Cedar Creek Walk - Easy, shaded trail following the creek through town. Pleasant in late afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: Day 4 - Central Park opens the day: 843 acres of designed nature in the heart of Manhattan. Focus on the south and center: the Mall and its elms, Bethesda Terrace and its angel, Bow Bridge, Strawberry Fields in Lennon's memory. Two hours on foot, much less with rental bike.

Day 4 - Belvedere Castle, the Alice in Wonderland statue, Lake rowboats: Central Park is practiced more than visited. A warning about today's deliberately dense program: two giant museums border the park and you'll have to choose. Save legs for the afternoon.

activities.text: Rental rowboat on the Lake or simple bagel eaten on a rock: the break is essential before attacking the museums.
West park exit toward the Natural History Museum: 600 m, about 8 min walk.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Explore Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site preserving the most remarkable concentration of ancient Pueblo architecture in North America. Between 850 and 1250 CE, Chaco Canyon served as the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of a vast regional network spanning thousands of square miles. Massive great houses containing hundreds of rooms and multiple stories demonstrate sophisticated engineering and astronomical knowledge.

Visit Pueblo Bonito, the largest and most famous of Chaco's great houses, featuring over 600 rooms arranged in a perfect D-shape aligned to celestial events. The precision construction using millions of carefully shaped sandstone blocks continues to amaze archaeologists and visitors alike. Petroglyphs throughout the canyon document the spiritual and practical knowledge of these ancient peoples.

activities.text: Discover Fajada Butte and the famous Sun Dagger, where spirals carved into rock create a solar calendar marking solstices and equinoxes with remarkable precision. The park's remote location far from light pollution makes it exceptional for stargazing, designated an International Dark Sky Park. Hiking trails connect major ruins while revealing the canyon's stark desert beauty.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Pueblo Culture, Volcanic Fields and White Sands

places.name: Chamberlain, SD

visits.text: Pull off I-90 at exit 263 and walk the keelboat-shaped balcony of the Lewis and Clark Welcome Center — the Missouri River spreads below you in both directions, and the replica of the Corps' 55-foot keelboat gives you the scale. Just outside, *Dignity: Of Earth and Sky* by sculptor Dale Lamphere rises 50 feet in stainless steel — a Lakota and Dakota woman with outstretched quilt-patterned wings, facing the river the expedition came up in 1804. The Akta Lakota Museum at St. Joseph's Indian School, two miles east, holds one of the most comprehensive collections of Lakota art and artifacts in the Great Plains. Free admission.

days_plan.itin_title: Lewis & Clark Trail: St. Louis to Great Falls, Retracing the 1804 Expedition
