visits.text: Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Explore America's most visited national park protecting 2,114 square kilometers of ancient mountains. The UNESCO World Heritage Site preserves old-growth forests, diverse wildlife including black bears, and over 2,100 kilometers of streams.

Cades Cove — Drive the 18-kilometer loop through this historic valley preserving 19th-century homesteads, churches, and grist mills. White-tailed deer, wild turkeys, and black bears frequent the meadows surrounded by mountains.
Clingmans Dome — Hike to the park's highest point at 2,025 meters for 360-degree views from the observation tower. The half-mile paved trail gains 100 meters elevation through spruce-fir forest.
Laurel Falls — Walk 4.2 kilometers roundtrip to this 24-meter waterfall, one of the park's most popular destinations. The paved trail follows a mountain stream through forest to the cascading falls.

activities.text: Wildlife watching — Scan for black bears, elk, and synchronous fireflies depending on season. Early morning and dusk offer best viewing in Cades Cove and Cataloochee Valley.
Gatlinburg strip exploration — Browse Appalachian crafts, moonshine tastings, and family attractions. The mountain resort town offers tourist amenities and Smoky Mountain access.

visits.text: Stroll along Georgetown's Front Street, the main corridor of this remarkably preserved historic district running parallel to the Sampit River. Eighteenth and nineteenth-century buildings frame the waterfront, creating one of the most relaxed and picturesque settings in the Lowcountry. The town's unhurried pace and architectural character transport visitors to an earlier era of Southern coastal life.

Visit the Rice Museum housed in the historic Old Market Building, examining the role of rice cultivation in shaping South Carolina's economy and culture. Georgetown once served as the center of the colonial rice industry, and the museum's exhibits illuminate this pivotal chapter of regional history. The Belltower overlooking the waterfront has become an iconic symbol of the town.

activities.text: Walk the Harborwalk Marina at sunset, where open waterfront paths provide views of the Sampit River and surrounding marshlands. The measured, unhurried atmosphere invites lingering strolls past historic buildings and working boats. Georgetown's authentic character offers an alternative to busier coastal destinations while maintaining easy access to surrounding beaches and natural areas.

places.name: Gettysburg, PA

visits.text: You begin your Gettysburg visit at the Museum and Visitor Center, the essential starting point for understanding the deadliest battle of the Civil War. From July 1 to 3, 1863, Union and Confederate armies clashed here on the hills and fields of Pennsylvania, leaving more than 51,000 dead, wounded, or missing in three days. The museum preserves the Cyclorama - a 360-degree panoramic painting 377 feet in circumference depicting Pickett's Charge on July 3. The introductory film, produced by History Channel, effectively prepares you for the battlefield visit. Book tickets online; the museum is open 8am to 5pm March through November, 9am to 4pm in winter.

The 9.4-square-mile Gettysburg battlefield is traversed by more than 40 miles of roads dotted with 1,300 monuments, 400 cannons, and 148 historic buildings, making it one of the largest outdoor sculpture collections in the world. You climb Little Round Top, the hill whose defense by Colonel Joshua Chamberlain on July 2 saved the Union line, then descend into the jagged rocks of Devil's Den, scene of fierce fighting by Confederate sharpshooters. The Virginia Memorial marks the starting position of Pickett's Charge, that desperate frontal assault across a mile of open field on July 3, which cost the Confederacy more than 6,000 men in less than an hour. Hire an official Licensed Battlefield Guide for a 2-hour car tour (about $80), or download the NPS app for a self-guided tour.

The Soldiers' National Cemetery, consecrated on November 19, 1863, is where Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address - one of the shortest and most powerful speeches in world political history, 272 words that redefined the meaning of the war and the nation. The cemetery holds more than 3,500 Union soldiers, including hundreds of unknowns identified by their state of origin. The headstones arranged in concentric semicircles create a particular solemnity. Come in late afternoon, when the tour buses have left and the place regains its calm - the low light on the rows of white stones is striking.

activities.text: The Gettysburg bike tour is a different experience from the car tour: you cross the same fields as the soldiers, you feel the slope of the hills, and you physically understand why Little Round Top was so strategic to hold, and why Pickett's Charge across a mile of open ground was a near-suicidal mission. GettysBike offers guided or self-guided tours with electric bikes for those wanting to conserve energy. The battlefield is dotted with interpretive signs and QR codes linked to the NPS app. Arrive early in the morning: battlefield roads are quiet before 9am and crossing the misty fields in the dawn light is memorable.

Gettysburg is reputed to be one of the most haunted towns in the United States, and it would be hard to doubt after three days of carnage on its soil. Candlelit Ghost Tours at night walk through downtown streets and around former field hospitals, recounting stories of soldiers who died on site and testimonies from current residents. Whether you believe in ghosts or not, the nighttime setting of historic downtown Gettysburg, its 19th-century houses, and the quality of historical narratives accompanying the paranormal anecdotes make the outing worthwhile.

visits.text: Alaska Marine Highway Ferry - The six-hour crossing from Valdez to Whittier traverses Prince William Sound aboard state-operated ferries that accommodate vehicles and passengers. This scenic voyage passes glaciers, forested islands, and abundant marine wildlife, with onboard naturalists during summer months providing interpretation.

Whittier - This unusual community exists almost entirely within two large buildings, a legacy of its WWII military origins. The town serves as a major port for Prince William Sound cruises and provides access to the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel, North America's longest combined highway-rail tunnel at 2.5 miles.

Portage Valley - The route from Whittier passes through this glacier-carved valley, with views of Portage Glacier from visitor facilities operated by the U.S. Forest Service. The receding glacier, which has retreated significantly in recent decades, offers a visible example of climate change impacts.

activities.text: Girdwood Resort Area - Nestled in the Chugach Mountains 40 miles south of Anchorage, this four-season resort community offers aerial tram rides to 2,300-foot elevation for panoramic views, hiking trails through temperate rainforest, and access to both alpine and coastal ecosystems.

visits.text: You pull into Makoshika State Park - the name comes from Lakota, meaning 'bad land' - and the landscape justifies it: hoodoos, caprocks, fluted hillsides, and natural bridges carved from Hell Creek Formation sandstone. Over ten dinosaur species have been found here, including T. rex and Triceratops. A 600-pound juvenile female Triceratops skull, excavated during a 1990-91 dig led by paleontologist Diane Gabriel, is on display at the visitor center. In 1997, Jack Horner and Bob Harmon found a nearly complete Thescelosaurus skeleton here. The K-T boundary line - the geological marker of the mass extinction 66 million years ago - is visible in the rock walls. Fee applies for non-Montana residents.

Stop at the Frontier Gateway Museum in downtown Glendive. It houses a full-size skeleton cast of 'Margie', a Struthiomimus found near Glendive, plus exhibits on the Yellowstone River, the town's railroad history, and the cattle era. William Clark described these badlands in his journal on July 30, 1806, calling them the 'birnt hills' - the pale sandstone cliffs visible today from the river. Free or low-cost admission.

Walk down to the Yellowstone River at Jaycee Park. This stretch is one of the best places in Montana to find Yellowstone agates - semi-precious stones formed in gas pockets in volcanic rock and polished over millennia by the current. The river is broad and shallow with sandbars good for wading; late summer exposes the most gravel. No permit required for personal quantities.

activities.text: Drive the Makoshika scenic road through the heart of the badlands and stop at Sand Creek Overlook and Artist Vista Overlook. The light changes the color of the formations dramatically throughout the day; late afternoon turns the rock faces from grey-brown to deep orange. The disc golf course runs right through the badlands, which gives a sense of scale even if you don't play. Passable by regular vehicle in dry conditions.

Go agate hunting on Yellowstone gravel bars east of Glendive. Look for stones with translucent banding or a waxy sheen at public river access sites maintained by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks. Bring wading shoes and a bucket. The best bars are exposed at low water in late summer. No permit required for personal quantities.

visits.text: Leave New Orleans via River Road (LA-18) heading west—this route follows the Mississippi for 75 miles between NOLA and Baton Rouge. Before the Civil War, this was one of America's wealthiest regions: sugarcane plantations stretched as far as the eye could see. First stop 30 miles out: Whitney Plantation in Wallace. This is Louisiana's only museum entirely dedicated to the history of slavery. Three memorials, period slave cabins, and an 1870 church built by freedmen tell the story of those who lived and worked here by force. The guided tour lasts 90 minutes—it's intense and necessary.

Continue 15 miles to Vacherie for Oak Alley Plantation, Louisiana's most famous. Its avenue of 28 live oaks planted in the early 18th century forms a quarter-mile vegetative tunnel between the road and the house. The Greek Revival mansion dates from 1839, built by Jacques Roman. Six replica slave cabins have been reconstructed based on archaeological excavations, and the walls bear the names of more than 220 people enslaved on this property between 1836 and 1865.

Four miles from Oak Alley, Laura Plantation offers a striking contrast. This is a Creole plantation—no white columns here, but a colorful cypress wood house raised on brick pillars in Louisiana vernacular style. The estate dates from 1805 and was managed by Creole women for four generations. The tour is narrated from the manuscript of Laura Locoul, born here in 1861. This is also where the Br'er Rabbit stories were collected, told by the plantation's Senegalese slaves.

activities.text: If you still have time, drive 3 miles south to San Francisco Plantation, the most colorful on River Road—its painted facade recalls New Orleans houses. Otherwise, head to Gonzales (30 minutes) for the night. Gonzales proclaims itself the "Jambalaya Capital of the World"—if you find a local restaurant open, order some and judge for yourself.

visits.text: Day 1 - Optional if time permits: Governors Island, a former military base turned park, a few minutes by boat from the Battery Maritime Building. The artificial hills of The Hills give a frontal view of the statue and harbor. Bike rentals, lawns, hammocks: the perfect breather after the morning lines.

Day 1 - Fort Jay and Castle Williams, two early 19th-century fortifications, are freely accessible on Governors Island. The island can be walked in a good hour. It closes early evening: check the last boat schedule before settling into the grass.

visits.text: Walk the Strip (36.111, -115.173) from Mandalay Bay in the south (36.0926, -115.1764) to the Stratosphere in the north (36.1473, -115.1561)—6.8 km, 45 minutes walking, several hours if you stop. The Venetian's gondolas (36.1211, -115.1700), indoor canals with singing gondoliers, cost $35-50 per couple and constitute the first degree of a staging of Venice that has never seen the sea. The High Roller (36.1175, -115.1683), the world's tallest observation wheel at its 2014 opening at 167 meters, gives panoramic views of the entire Strip from above, $28.

Go down to Fremont Street Experience (36.1707, -115.1437)—old Las Vegas from the 1940s-1950s, a street covered by a 460-meter LED screen, the Viva Vision Canopy, the world's largest. Light shows trigger every hour from 6 PM to 1 AM. The Golden Nugget and Binion's are the historic founding casinos, less flashy than the Strip and more honest about what they are.

Go up the Stratosphere Tower (36.1473, -115.1561)—350 meters, five thrill rides at the top including the X-Scream that tilts over the edge and the SkyJump at 261 meters. View of the entire Strip from a height that other towers don't give. For those who prefer to stay below, the nighttime view from the sidewalk at the tower's base is enough to understand the scale of it all.

activities.text: Leave for the Grand Canyon early afternoon—4.5 hours via I-40 then AZ-64. Hotels inside the park (El Tovar Hotel, Bright Angel Lodge) book 6 to 12 months in advance; otherwise, Tusayan south of the park for $150-280/night. Arrive at Mather Point (36.0617, -112.1083) for sunset—180° panoramic view, raking light revealing geological layers.

Have dinner on the Strip before leaving—Las Vegas hosts restaurants by Michelin-starred chefs (Joël Robuchon at MGM Grand, Guy Savoy at Caesars Palace) at prices that remain lower than their Parisian addresses. Casino buffets cover the other end: $15-50 depending on level. What Las Vegas doesn't do well is mid-range.

visits.text: Day 3 - Under Grand Central Terminal's turquoise vault, 2,500 painted stars overhang the commuter ballet. The hall crosses freely, at any hour. Look for the Whispering Gallery in front of the Oyster Bar: two people at opposite corners can hear each other whisper across the vault.

Day 3 - Grand Central hides a gourmet market, basement food court, and the central kiosk's four-faced clock, quintessential New York meeting point. Pass through at rush hour, 8-9 AM or 5-6 PM: the station then plays its true score. Fifteen minutes of guaranteed spectacle.

activities.text: Oysters at the Grand Central Oyster Bar counter, opened in 1913 under its Guastavino ceramic vaults: not cheap, but memorable by the half-dozen.

places.name: Grand Island, NE

visits.text: The Stuhr Museum of the Prairie Pioneer sprawls across 200 acres southwest of Grand Island and is one of the most ambitious living history complexes in the Midwest. The centerpiece is Railroad Town - over 60 original structures relocated from across the Great Plains to recreate an 1890s prairie village complete with a blacksmith, a church, a general store, a Pawnee earth lodge, and the birthplace of Henry Fonda (born here in 1905; he personally helped relocate and restore the house in 1966). The circular Stuhr Building was designed by Edward Durell Stone - the architect of the Kennedy Center - opened in 1967 on a surrounding moat. Costumed interpreters bring the town to life from May through September. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015. Paid entry.

The Crane Trust Nature and Visitor Center, west of Grand Island along the Platte River, sits at the center of one of the world's great wildlife events. Each spring - mid-February to mid-April, peaking in late March - over one million sandhill cranes converge on a 70-mile stretch of the Platte, representing more than 80 percent of the world population. Fossil records place cranes in Nebraska for nine million years, predating the Platte River itself. Each individual bird stays about 29 days, consuming nearly 1,600 tons of waste corn before continuing to Canadian and Alaskan breeding grounds. Guided sunrise and sunset tours during migration sell out weeks ahead - book early at the Crane Trust website.

activities.text: At dawn, drive 20 miles west to Kearney and watch cranes from the free public viewpoints: the Fort Kearny hike-bike trail bridge or the Plautz Crane Viewing Platform south of Gibbon. During peak migration in March, the pre-dawn silence gives way to the rolling rattle of hundreds of thousands of birds; the mass lift-off at sunrise can blot out the sky. At dusk, they pour back to the river in a stream that lasts an hour, silhouetted against the setting sun. Outside migration season, the Platte corridor is still productive for pelicans, herons and migrating waterfowl.

After the Stuhr Museum, take the route along the Platte's south bank back toward Grand Island - the river is shallow, braided and wide here, and herons, white pelicans and deer are routine sightings from roadside pulloffs. Stolley Park on the west edge of Grand Island is a quiet spot for a riverside picnic before dinner. The downtown holds several well-preserved late 19th-century commercial blocks and reliable local restaurants.

places.name: Grand Junction, CO

visits.text: Start at Colorado National Monument, just outside Fruita. Rim Rock Drive winds 23 miles along red sandstone cliffs carved by millions of years of erosion. Stop at Independence Monument View—this 450-foot monolith is the park's tallest, and every Fourth of July a flag is raised at its summit. If you only have time for one short hike, take Otto's Trail (1-mile round trip): the plunging canyon views are worth every step.

Late in the day, cruise through downtown Grand Junction. This is mainly your chance to fuel up and stock water—once you pass Green River, services become scarce. Also locate a grocery store to pack picnic supplies for the coming days.

Before heading back to Grand Junction, allow yourself one last stop at Chimney Rock, visible from Highway 24 at the park's western entrance. This ochre sandstone chimney capped with a darker rock hat is one of Capitol Reef's icons. A 3.6-mile loop trail circles the formation—the view from the top embraces the entire Waterpocket Fold.

On Highway 24 heading east, spot the Behunin Cabin right by the roadside. Built in 1882 by Elijah Behunin from red sandstone to blend into the landscape, this tiny one-room cabin sheltered a family of 13. The stop takes only a few minutes but the story is worth the detour.

The return via I-70 crosses the San Rafael Swell—and this stretch of highway is spectacular in itself. For about 30 miles, the road cuts through geologic cross-sections of red and gray sandstone, with cliffs on either side. Several rest areas offer viewpoints. Take time to stop before returning to Grand Junction.

activities.text: If you're a cyclist, Rim Rock Drive is considered one of Colorado's finest road-biking routes—locals call it the "Tour of the Moon." Otherwise, take a short walk from the Saddlehorn Visitor Center to watch desert bighorn sheep that populate the cliffs.

If your flight or plans allow, save 1.5 hours at day's end for another pass through Colorado National Monument on the Fruita side—this time in late-afternoon light. The sandstone colors change completely compared to the morning of Day 1. The Devil's Kitchen Trail (1.5 miles) is a good option for a final short hike.

places.name: Grand Lake, CO

visits.text: The day is dominated by crossing Trail Ridge Road, the highest continuous paved road in the United States at 12,183 feet elevation. Over 48 miles total (including 11 miles above 11,000 feet), it connects Estes Park to Grand Lake by crossing the Continental Divide. Built from 1929 to 1938 by the Civilian Conservation Corps, it receives up to 25 feet of snow in winter and requires an average of 42 days of snow removal each spring at a cost exceeding $30,000. Stop at Rainbow Curve (10,829 feet) for the view over the glacial valley, then at the Alpine Visitor Center (11,796 feet) - the highest National Park Service visitor center in the United States. Bring a jacket even in summer: temperatures at the summit are often 20°F colder than in Denver.

On the west side, the Kawuneeche Valley follows the headwaters of the Colorado River - the river that irrigates seven states and provides water to 40 million people originates in this park. Stop at the Kawuneeche Visitor Center, then watch for elk and moose in the meadows bordering the river. The Holzwarth Historic Site, accessible from a parking lot just north of the center, preserves cabins from a 1917 ranch - one of the country's first dude ranches.

Grand Lake, founded in 1881, is Colorado's largest natural lake with a maximum depth exceeding 380 feet. The small town counts fewer than 500 permanent residents but its boardwalk concentrates shops and restaurants with no chains - it's one of the few small Colorado mountain towns to have resisted commercial standardization. Late afternoon, take the short walk to Point Park for panoramic views of the lake and surrounding peaks.

activities.text: Rent a kayak or canoe on Grand Lake - the Grand Lake Yacht Club, founded in 1902, is one of the world's highest yacht clubs at 8,369 feet elevation. You can also take a motorboat to explore the two connected lakes, Grand Lake and Shadow Mountain Lake. Rental outfitters offer kayaks and boats by the hour or day from lakeside marinas.

places.name: Grand Marais, MN

visits.text: Grand Marais sits on a natural double harbor 40 miles from the Canadian border, between the Sawtooth Mountains and Lake Superior. The Ojibwe called it Gitchi-Ba-Too-Biig, the double bay. Budget Travel Magazine named it America's Coolest Small Town. Downtown spans three blocks around Harbor Park—art galleries, artisan shops, seafood restaurants—with the lake as a constant horizon.

Walk out to Artist's Point, the rocky promontory jutting into the lake east of town. From the point, you overlook both harbor basins on one side and the vastness of Lake Superior on the other. In bad weather, waves crash just feet away—the atmosphere completely transforms. The walk from the harbor parking lot takes 15 minutes.

activities.text: The North House Folk School, established on the lakeshore since 1997, offers workshops in blacksmithing, timber framing, basketry, bread baking, or birch-bark canoe building. If your timing lines up with a one-day workshop, sign up: it's one of the most authentic North Shore experiences. Otherwise, browse the shop and tour the campus.

visits.text: Great Bend and Cheyenne Bottoms - North America's Most Important Bird Migration Route: Arrive at sunrise to witness one of nature's greatest spectacles as hundreds of thousands of birds utilize this critical stopover on their continental journeys.

Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area - The Largest Inland Wetland in the United States: This 41,000-acre complex of marshy basins provides the richest wetland feeding grounds in the central flyway, critical to the survival of some 320 bird species that frequent these waters.

Kansas Wetlands Education Center - Understanding an Ecological Treasure: Exhibits explain the international importance of this freshwater marsh and its role in supporting migrating waterfowl and shorebirds each spring and autumn.

Quivira National Wildlife Refuge - A Rare Inland Saltwater Marsh: Just south of Great Bend, this unusual Midwest ecosystem features trails leading to closer views of ducks, geese, and several endangered species in a landscape unlike anywhere else in Kansas.

activities.text: Sunrise Birding - Watch Pelicans Take Flight: Time your visit for dawn to observe pods of American white pelicans lifting off the water, beginning another day of their remarkable migration.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Prairie Odyssey: Tallgrass Seas, Cowtowns & Western Legends

places.name: Great Falls, MT

visits.text: The Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail Interpretive Center is built into a bluff overlooking the Missouri, and the Corps spent more time here than anywhere outside of winter camp. The portage of five successive waterfalls took 33 days in June and July 1805, covering 18 miles on improvised log-wheeled wagons through prickly pear cactus, grizzly bear territory, and flash-flooding coulees. The 25,000-square-foot center's centerpiece is a two-story diorama of the portage; you can test your strength on a simulated boat-hauling station. An actor-portrayed 45-minute audio walk reconstructs the scene in William Clark's voice. Paid entry ($8 adults); closed Mondays and Tuesdays outside peak season.

Giant Springs Heritage State Park is a quarter-mile walk from the Interpretive Center along the River's Edge Trail, and it holds one of the largest freshwater springs in the world. Lewis described it on June 18, 1805 as 'a most beautiful fountain' — the spring discharges at 156 million gallons per day through limestone. The Roe River, flowing just 200 feet from the spring to the Missouri, long claimed the title of the world's shortest river — a distinction that has since been contested and removed from the Guinness records. The park has picnic areas, trout ponds, and a wildlife center. Free admission.

The C.M. Russell Museum covers an entire city block and holds close to 1,000 original works by Charles Marion Russell — painter, sculptor, and self-described cowboy who arrived in Montana at age 16 in 1880 and spent the rest of his life documenting the West before it vanished. His log cabin studio, built in 1903 from western red cedar telephone poles, stands on the museum grounds alongside his family home — both National Historic Landmarks since 1965. More than 3,000 pieces of Western art fill 16 galleries. Paid entry; open daily in summer.

activities.text: The River's Edge Trail runs 60 miles of paved non-motorized path through Great Falls along the Missouri, connecting the Interpretive Center to Giant Springs, the five waterfall overlooks, and the CMR Museum district. Rent a bike in town and ride the section from Giant Springs past Rainbow Falls and Black Eagle Dam — about 8 miles of riverside trail with the actual waterfalls that stopped the Corps for 33 days. The falls look modest now, controlled by power dams, but the side canyons and cottonwood banks still tell the story.

First Peoples Buffalo Jump State Park, 10 miles south of Great Falls off I-15, is a mile-long sandstone cliff where Indigenous hunters drove bison for at least 2,000 years — the remains of millions of processed animals lie in the talus below. An interpretive trail and shelter explain the archaeology. It predates Lewis and Clark by millennia, but it gives the Great Falls stop a deeper Indigenous context that the expedition barely acknowledged during its grueling month-long portage. Free admission; 30-minute drive from downtown.

places.name: Green Bay, WI

visits.text: Green Bay is the smallest city in the United States to own an NFL franchise - the Packers, founded in 1919, are also the only professional football team collectively owned by its fans (approximately 360,000 shareholders). Lambeau Field, inaugurated in 1957 and expanded to 81,441 seats, remains one of the league's most legendary stadiums. On non-game days, the guided stadium and Packers Hall of Fame tour lasts 1h30 - you enter the locker rooms, walk on the field, and touch a replica Lombardi Trophy. Book online if visiting during season (September to January).

The National Railroad Museum in Green Bay assembles one of the largest collections of locomotives and railcars in the United States, including the Union Pacific's Big Boy - the largest steam locomotive ever built, 132 tons, put into service in 1941. You can board several restored railcars, including Eisenhower's presidential car used during World War II. Count on 1h30 to complete the outdoor yard and indoor exhibitions.

The CityDeck runs along the Fox River right in downtown Green Bay - a wooden boardwalk over the water with restaurant patios and benches facing the evening reflections. This is where locals gather after work, far from the Lambeau Field excitement. Take advantage to dine on the riverfront before tomorrow's long leg to the Upper Peninsula.

activities.text: The Bay Beach Wildlife Sanctuary spans 280 hectares bordering Green Bay. This municipal refuge shelters deer, foxes, otters and injured raptors under rehabilitation - all observable from free marked trails. It's one of the rare urban green spaces where you can find yourself alone with nature less than 5 minutes from downtown. Go in late afternoon for the best observation chances.

Green Bay is the perfect meeting point between Wisconsin's two prides: beer and cheese. Downtown bars serve local craft beers accompanied by regional creamery cheeses - aged cheddar, colby, and the curious cheese curd, fresh cheese balls that squeak under the tooth. A simple and authentic way to close the day before the big transit to the Upper Peninsula tomorrow morning.

places.name: Green River, UT

visits.text: Drive to Wedge Overlook, nicknamed Utah's "Little Grand Canyon." At the end of a well-maintained dirt road (passable in a regular car in dry weather), you'll reach the edge of a 1,200-foot drop above the San Rafael River. The panorama is staggering—and you'll likely be alone staring into the void. No services on-site, no water, no safety barriers.

On your way down through Buckhorn Draw, stop at the Buckhorn Wash Pictograph Panel. This Barrier Canyon–style rock art dates back more than 2,000 years—the life-size figures are among the most impressive in the Colorado Plateau. The site is accessible right from the road, about 3 miles north of the San Rafael River bridge.

In Green River, step inside the John Wesley Powell River History Museum, perched on the riverbank. Don't miss the 25-minute film "The Great Unknown," which traces Powell's 1869 expedition—three months and 1,000 miles on rivers no one had ever mapped. Downstairs you'll find replicas of period boats and a small dinosaur exhibit.

activities.text: Green River is Utah's melon capital. If you're passing through in September, the Melon Days Festival is in full swing. Year-round, it's also the launch point for kayak or raft trips on the Green River—the Desolation Canyon stretch offers Class I–II rapids accessible to beginners.

visits.text: Day 5 - Atypical option yet one of Brooklyn's most beautiful walks: Green-Wood Cemetery, 1838 garden cemetery, hills, ponds, and mausoleums under century-old trees. Basquiat, Leonard Bernstein, and Boss Tweed rest here. Free admission through the 25th Street neo-Gothic portal, where green parakeets nest.

Day 5 - From Battle Hill, Brooklyn's highest point in Green-Wood's heart, Minerva's statue salutes the Statue of Liberty straight in the eye, harbor below. In the 19th century, the place drew more visitors than anyone before Central Park. Free maps at entrance, trolley tours certain days.

activities.text: Count 1 to 1.5 hours of quiet walking; in strong heat, it's also the coolest spot in Day 5's program.

visits.text: Moosehead Lake is the largest lake in New England - 40 miles long, up to 20 miles wide, and sitting at 1,023 feet of elevation in the boreal forest. Greenville perches at its southern tip, and from the public boat launch you can see Mount Kineo, an 800-foot rhyolite cliff that erupts from the water near the middle of the lake. The waterfront downtown is small but purposeful: outfitters, a diner, and Northwoods Outfitters - the main gear and guide hub for the region. Arrive before dusk and drive Lily Bay Road north of town - moose are frequently spotted in the ditches and beaver ponds along this stretch.

Berthed at the town dock, the SS Katahdin - locally called 'the Kate' - is the oldest vessel afloat built at Bath Iron Works, launched in 1914. She carried tourists and supplies to the Mount Kineo Resort, then spent decades as a lumber towboat hauling log booms across the lake until 1975. The Moosehead Marine Museum rescued her in 1976 and restored her completely in the 1990s, including replating the hull at Bath Iron Works. She runs cruises from June through October - the three-hour version goes north past Beaver Cove and Sugar Island, with narration on the lake's history and wildlife.

Lily Bay State Park sits 9 miles north of Greenville on the eastern shore of Moosehead Lake. The 952-acre park has lakefront campsites that rank among the most scenic in New England, plus a small swimming beach, hiking trails, and boat launch. Even on a day visit, the views across the lake toward Squaw Mountain are worth the trip. Open year-round; summer brings paddlers and anglers, winter brings snowshoers and cross-country skiers.

activities.text: Northwoods Outfitters on Lily Bay Road runs the moose safaris that Yankee Magazine voted best in New England. Registered Maine Guides take small private groups out at dawn and dusk - the times when moose are most active - either by vehicle on logging roads or by canoe on remote beaver ponds. Success rates are high: guides claim over 1,000 sightings a year. Book the early-morning tour for the best light and the highest probability of seeing bulls.

If the seaplanes at Currier's Flying Service catch your eye at the town dock, a 30-minute floatplane flight over Moosehead Lake makes the wilderness scale unmistakable - 40 miles of lake surrounded by nothing but boreal forest stretching to the Canadian border. Currier's has been operating bush-flying charters out of Greenville since 1947, making it one of the oldest floatplane operations in the Northeast.

days_plan.itin_title: Inland Maine: Moosehead Lake, Mount Katahdin & the North Woods

visits.text: Leland, 10 miles east of Greenville on Highway 61, produced Jimmy Reed, Little Milton, Eddie Cusic, and blues-rock guitarist Johnny Winter, whose father ran a local cotton business. The Highway 61 Blues Museum on the main drag covers around 80 Delta blues artists from the surrounding area, with instruments, photographs, and hand-annotated festival posters. Blues musician Son Thomas lived here for decades; his son Pat Thomas still plays in the museum most days, unpaid and purely for love of the music. Leland is also Jim Henson's hometown - the Kermit the Frog exhibit is next door if the kids need a break.

Robert Johnson recorded 'They're Red Hot' about tamales in 1936, and that tradition runs deep. Greenville, which declared itself the Hot Tamale Capital of the World in 2012, is the best place in the Delta to taste it. Delta tamales are smaller than Mexican ones, made with cornmeal instead of masa, heavily spiced, and simmered rather than steamed - the recipe most likely crossed between Mexican migrant farm workers and Black laborers in the cotton fields in the early 20th century. Scott's Hot Tamales on MLK Boulevard uses a family recipe dating to 1950, wrapping each one by hand in corn shucks. Doe's Eat Place on Nelson Street has served tamales alongside its steaks since the 1940s. Budget an hour for lunch.

activities.text: The drive south from Clarksdale on Highway 61 is itself a full activity: flat Delta farmland, bayous, shotgun houses, grain elevators, Mississippi Blues Trail markers appearing every few miles. Stop at each one - they're brief, factual, and densely specific, each giving a name, a date, a story. By the time you reach Greenville you'll have covered the arc from Charley Patton through the Great Migration. Keep the windows down and drive slowly; the light over Delta cotton fields in morning hours is worth photographing.

Lake Washington, 20 miles east of Greenville, is an oxbow lake - one of the crescent-shaped bodies of water left when the Mississippi River shifted course. Blues musicians played around its shores for generations, and the surrounding county roads look largely unchanged from the sharecropping era. An evening drive around the lake, stopping to look at the old plantation structures, closes the day with a quieter look at the landscape that produced all this music. Pack mosquito repellent between May and September.

days_plan.itin_title: Mississippi Delta Blues Trail: Memphis to Jackson

visits.text: Marvel at Falls Park on the Reedy, an urban oasis where the Reedy River tumbles over a dramatic waterfall surrounded by gardens, stone pathways, and shady trees in the heart of downtown Greenville. The curved Liberty Bridge suspension walkway floats above the falls, offering sweeping views that never fail to impress. This transformed space represents one of the finest urban parks in the American South.

Stroll along the Swamp Rabbit Trail, miles of scenic pathway following the Reedy River through beautiful natural areas and charming neighborhoods. The trail connects downtown attractions to outlying communities, providing opportunities for walking, running, and cycling. Greenville's investment in green spaces and pedestrian infrastructure has created a remarkably livable city.

activities.text: Explore downtown Greenville's wide, walkable streets lined with boutique shops, art galleries, and diverse dining options. The city's vibrant arts scene includes world-class performances and exhibitions throughout the year. Flowering gardens, hidden nooks, and benches overlooking the river invite visitors to slow down and appreciate this mountain-ringed cultural destination.

days_plan.itin_title: South Carolina Grand Tour: Charleston to Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Greenwich - Where New York Sophistication Meets New England Charm: This affluent coastal community on Connecticut's Gold Coast offers pristine beaches, world-class shopping, and stunning waterfront estates. The town's 32-mile shoreline along Long Island Sound provides endless opportunities for sailing, swimming, and scenic strolls.

Bruce Museum - Science and Art Under One Roof: This regional museum showcases natural history, environmental science, and fine arts through rotating exhibitions and permanent collections that illuminate both the natural world and human creativity.

activities.text: Greenwich Avenue Shopping District - The Rodeo Drive of Connecticut: Browse upscale boutiques, galleries, and gourmet food shops along this tree-lined thoroughfare that has attracted discerning shoppers for over a century.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Coastal Drive: From Maritime Mystic to Ivy League New Haven

visits.text: Conquer Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas at 8,751 feet, where breathtaking panoramic views reward determined hikers who complete the challenging summit trail. This ancient fossilized reef mountain, dating back over 260 million years, rises dramatically from the Chihuahuan Desert floor. Standing atop Texas provides an unparalleled sense of accomplishment and connection to the state's geological heritage.

Discover McKittrick Canyon, renowned for producing the most spectacular fall foliage display in West Texas when maples, oaks, and other deciduous trees transform the desert canyon into a blaze of autumn colors. The canyon's unique microclimate supports a surprisingly diverse ecosystem within the arid surrounding landscape. Crystal-clear streams and towering limestone walls create a hidden oasis that contrasts dramatically with the desert terrain.

activities.text: Hike the El Capitan trail for closer views of the park's iconic rocky outcrop, a massive limestone cliff that served as a landmark for travelers, including Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoaches, crossing the desert for centuries. The park offers exceptional stargazing opportunities due to minimal light pollution from surrounding areas. Over 300 species of birds have been documented here, making it a premier destination for wildlife observation.

days_plan.itin_title: Discovering Texas: Hill Country, Big Bend & Gulf Coast Beaches

visits.text: Day 4 - Frank Lloyd Wright's white spiral is worth as much as its collections: at the Guggenheim, you ride the elevator up and descend the gentle ramp, works scrolling over 1,300 feet. $30 ticket. After the Met or Museum, an hour's overview amply suffices; the architecture does the rest.

Day 4 - The Guggenheim deploys Kandinsky in depth, the Impressionists of the Thannhauser collection, and major temporary exhibitions in the rotunda. Certain evenings offer pay-what-you-wish slots, check online. The 1959 building photographs from outside with a wide angle, from the sidewalk across the street.

activities.text: If museum saturation threatens, skip the interior without remorse: façade, photo, and head straight to Harlem for a change of air.
Subway to Harlem: 3.1 km, 4/5/6 lines from 86th Street station to 125th Street, about 20 min walk included.

visits.text: Jour 1: Trade city streets for coastal paradise as you enter Gulf State Park, a 6,000-acre sanctuary where pristine white-sand beaches meet freshwater lakes teeming with wildlife. Rent a bike at Lake Shelby and pedal along trails crossing bridges between three interconnected lakes, pausing at the Nature Centre to learn about the alligators, herons, and sea turtles that call this preserve home. The Leave Only Footprints program protects nesting sea turtles along the shore.

Jour 1: Sink your toes into the sugary sand of Gulf Shores Beach, where the Gulf of Mexico's emerald waters lap against Alabama's stunning 60-mile coastline. Unlike the crowded shores of neighboring Florida, these beaches offer space to breathe, with the state park providing particularly peaceful stretches backed by natural dunes rather than high-rise condos. A long fishing pier attracts anglers casting for the day's catch.

Jour 1: Experience coastal luxury with a conscience at The Lodge at Gulf State Park, a striking wood-clad hotel run by Hilton but owned by Alabama, with all proceeds supporting state parks. Book a beach-view lunch at Foodcraft restaurant, where sustainable Southern cuisine celebrates local ingredients in a light-filled setting overlooking the dunes. Even day visitors can access the hotel's pristine stretch of protected beach.

Jour 2: Set sail with Cetacean Cruises for an afternoon dolphin encounter, where bottlenose dolphins play in the wake of your vessel as you glide through the calm waters of Mobile Bay. The knowledgeable crew shares fascinating facts about these intelligent marine mammals while steering toward shrimp boats where dolphins congregate for easy meals. With the sail raised and a drink in hand, there's no better way to experience Alabama's coastal waters.

Jour 2: Drive the scenic coastal route to Fort Morgan, a star-shaped brick fortress guarding the mouth of Mobile Bay since the 1830s. This strategic stronghold witnessed fierce Civil War naval battles, including Admiral Farragut's famous cry to damn the torpedoes. Climb the ramparts for sweeping views across the bay to Dauphin Island, where its sister Fort Gaines stands sentinel on the opposite shore.

Jour 2: Board the Mobile Bay Ferry for a scenic cruise to Dauphin Island, where Fort Gaines and quiet beaches await exploration. The 35-minute crossing offers dolphin spotting opportunities and gorgeous views of both fortifications that once defended this vital waterway. History buffs can explore the companion fort before catching the return ferry.

activities.text: Jour 1: Start your beach day right at Woodside Restaurant, a laid-back cafe on the edge of Gulf State Park where the South Island Parfait layers fresh tropical fruit and banana bread with creamy Greek yogurt drizzled in local honey. The setting amid the park's natural beauty makes this more than just breakfast, it's the beginning of an adventure.

Jour 1: Embrace beach club vibes at The Gulf, a buzzing waterfront gathering spot built from repurposed shipping containers painted in cheerful colors. Order shrimp tacos and fresh-squeezed lemonade from one of two outdoor kitchens, then claim a table overlooking the water as the sun begins its descent. Families, friends, and the occasional live band create an atmosphere that captures everything wonderful about Alabama's coast.

Jour 1: Dress for a special evening at Cobalt, where an expansive patio overlooks Perdido Bay and the menu showcases Gulf seafood at its finest. The tuna salad features ruby-red fish barely kissed by heat, scattered over greens with goat cheese, pecans, and house-pickled vegetables. The BBQ Gulf Shrimp swimming in butter sauce demands crusty bread for sopping every drop.

Jour 2: Settle into the boutique Hotel Indigo Orange Beach, a stylish retreat just steps from the sand where ocean-hued decor and a minimum check-in age of 25 ensure peaceful relaxation. The suite-style rooms include full living areas and kitchenettes that feel like your own beach apartment, while the pool and lobby swings invite lingering. The Backcountry Trail begins just behind the property for morning bike rides.

Jour 2: Browse for coastal treasures at Southern Grind Cafe next door to Hotel Indigo, where excellent coffee pairs with an eclectic collection of beach-inspired gifts and homeware. The dog-friendly patio welcomes four-legged travelers, while the cafe's breakfast and brunch offerings provide fuel for another day of Gulf Coast adventures.

Jour 2: Reflect on your Deep South journey as the sun sinks into the Gulf of Mexico, painting the sky in shades of peach and amber. From rocket ships to civil rights landmarks, recording studios to sugar-sand beaches, Alabama has revealed itself as so much more than a flyover state. The Heart of Dixie beats with stories of innovation, courage, creativity, and hospitality that will stay with you long after you've returned home.

days_plan.itin_title: Alabama Deep South Itinerary: Civil Rights, Music and Gulf Coast

places.name: Gustavus, AK

visits.text: The Bartlett Cove Visitor Center—9 miles from Gustavus via the area's only paved road—is NPS headquarters for Glacier Bay. Rangers give daily talks on the bay's extraordinary history: 250 years ago, everything was under 5,000 feet of ice. When Vancouver passed in 1794, the bay was largely filled with glaciers—he saw only a narrow arm of the sea at its entrance. Today the bay extends nearly 65 miles—making it one of the fastest glacial retreats ever documented on Earth.

The Forest Loop Trail (0.8 miles) and Bartlett River Trail (5 miles round-trip) both start from the Visitor Center through a forest of hemlock and spruce recently colonized on old moraines. The phenomenon of plant succession is visible to the naked eye: you pass from bare rock to moss, then to young trees in the span of a few hundred yards—a living geology lesson.

Point Adolphus, at the mouth of Icy Strait across from the village of Hoonah, is one of the most renowned humpback whale watching spots in North America. More than 85 humpback whales return each summer to these waters extremely rich in krill and fish. Local boats from Gustavus get you there in 30 minutes. Group bubble-net feeding displays—a cooperative hunting behavior where several whales blow a curtain of bubbles together to trap prey—are observed almost daily in July-August.

The Nagoonberry Loop Trail from Gustavus, an easy 3-mile trail through forests and coastal meadows, gives a sense of the region's unique rural landscape—Gustavus is one of the few Southeast Alaska communities where people grow vegetable gardens and houses have actual lawns. Wild raspberries and nagoonberries grow trailside. Views of the Fairweather Range peaks at the head of the bay are constant.

activities.text: The day-long bay cruise, organized by NPS aboard the catamaran Spirit of Adventure, ascends 65 miles to the Grand Pacific and Margerie glaciers at the head of the bay. A ranger-naturalist narrates the wildlife and geology throughout the crossing. Bears, wolves, mountain goats, porpoises, and up to a hundred species of seabirds are frequently spotted. Calving seracs from the face of Margerie Glacier create waves perceptible onboard.

Kayaking from Bartlett Cove with Glacier Bay Sea Kayaks—an hour or two of paddling is enough to escape all human presence into quiet coves where seals rest onshore. Guided introductions are offered for non-paddlers, as well as independent rentals for experienced kayakers. Don't venture into the upper reaches of the bay without experience and radio communication.

Sport fishing in Icy Strait targets halibut and coho salmon from late June through September—the depths of the strait are among the richest in the Inside Passage. Local charters depart from Gustavus dock and provide all gear. If you're not an angler, the marine wildlife en route—sea otters, Dall's porpoises, harbor seals—is more than enough for a morning on the water.

Bike from Gustavus to Bartlett Cove—the 9 miles of flat road between the two are ideal for observing meadows, wetlands, and transition forests. Local homeowners rent bikes by the day. Gustavus is one of Alaska's flattest and most bikeable places—take advantage, it's rare.

visits.text: The drive from Cincinnati is 746 miles—the longest leg of the trip. Leave at dawn. You'll cross Indiana, Illinois, and Missouri before entering Oklahoma. In the final stretches through Missouri and Oklahoma, I-44 parallels historic Route 66—watch for "Historic Route 66" signs and vintage gas stations along the roadside.

Guthrie is a town of 12,000 frozen in time. It was Oklahoma's first capital from 1890 to 1910, before losing that status to Oklahoma City overnight—residents woke up without their capital. The Victorian brick downtown is listed on the National Register and spans 400 buildings. Stroll along Harrison Avenue and Oklahoma Avenue.

Don't miss the Scottish Rite Masonic Temple, a massive neoclassical building that seems incongruous in a town this size. Built in 1919, it's one of the world's largest Masonic temples. The interior is open for tours—the painted ceilings and pipe organs are worth seeing.

activities.text: Guthrie is also the "bluegrass capital of the world." If you're there on a Friday or Saturday night, there's often live music at the bars on Harrison Avenue. Otherwise, enjoy the quiet—you're far from everything here, and that's the point.

days_plan.itin_title: The Rain Man Route: An American Road Trip

visits.text: The skull of a Hagerman Horse dominates the visitor center at Hagerman Fossil Beds - Equus simplicidens, Idaho's state fossil, the earliest known member of the genus Equus. Rancher Elmer Cook spotted bones eroding from the bluffs along the Snake River in 1928 and called the U.S. Geological Survey; the Smithsonian dug here from 1929 to 1934 and uncovered more than 200 individual horse specimens of all ages and both sexes, alongside mastodons, saber-toothed cats, and ground sloths, all 3 to 4 million years old. The fragile sandstone bluffs are restricted; the visitor center is the place to see the fossils. Free admission.

The Oregon Trail emigrants who passed through this valley in the 1840s and 1850s stopped and stared: springs poured straight out of the canyon walls by the dozens, cascading down basalt cliffs into the Snake River below. They were looking at overflow from the Snake River Plain Aquifer, recharged every year by snowmelt from the Rocky Mountains above. At Malad Gorge today, the Malad River drops through stairstep falls into the Devil's Washbowl then cuts a 250-foot gorge; the bridge crossing it gives you the best view. One park fee ($7) covers all six units of Thousand Springs State Park.

Ritter Island sits in the Snake River as a green anomaly - surrounded by water and canyon walls, with Lemon Falls cascading into view on all sides. In the early 20th century, Minnie Miller ran a state-of-the-art Guernsey dairy farm here; her original buildings are still standing. The Nature Conservancy bought the 385-acre property in 1986. Access is Thursday through Monday, Memorial Day through Labor Day; a rental house on the island is bookable year-round through Idaho State Parks.

activities.text: Hagerman's stretch of the Snake River runs Class I-III whitewater through a canyon whose walls are the same fossil-bearing bluffs you visited this morning. Several local outfitters run guided half-day trips with the fossils above you the whole time. For something quieter, the Billingsley Creek unit of Thousand Springs State Park has excellent fly-fishing - the creek is fed by constant-temperature springs and stocked with trout year-round.

Clear Springs Foods, headquartered just outside Hagerman, is one of the largest commercial trout producers in North America - so the fish at local restaurants is as fresh as it gets. The Hagerman Valley Inn handles dinner well. For breakfast, Bullets N' Brews is exactly what the name suggests: espresso and breakfast burritos alongside shelves of ammunition, which is more normal in rural Idaho than it sounds.

days_plan.itin_title: Idaho: Sawtooth Mountains, Sun Valley & Craters of the Moon

visits.text: Goblin Valley State Park is one of Utah's strangest places. Across roughly 2 square miles, thousands of sandstone mushrooms—the "goblins"—stand in a landscape that served as the set for the film Galaxy Quest. These formations were born from erosion of the Entrada Sandstone, deposited 170 million years ago when the region bordered an ancient sea. Unlike most parks, you can wander freely among the hoodoos. Arrive in the morning—on weekends and school holidays, the parking lot fills fast.

Don't leave the area without seeing the Three Sisters, the park's most photographed trio of hoodoos. A short marked trail runs from the access road to the viewpoint. From the main overlook, descend the stairs into the "first valley" and lose yourself among the formations—the farther south you go, the taller the goblins grow.

Factory Butte is visible from Highway 24, about 12 miles west of Hanksville. This isolated monolith rises to 6,300 feet and dominates an ocean of blue-gray badlands streaked with yellow. Come at sunrise or sunset—the raking light transforms the ravines into an abstract painting. The access road (Factory Butte Road) is passable in dry weather, but the slightest rain turns the clay into a vehicle trap.

activities.text: Five miles from Goblin Valley's entrance, Little Wild Horse Canyon is one of Utah's best accessible slot canyons. No technical gear required: the 3.1-mile round-trip trail winds between sandstone walls so narrow you sometimes have to pass sideways. Allow 2 to 3 hours. For the more ambitious, the full loop with Bell Canyon is 8 miles and about 4 hours. Check the weather before you go—if there's any chance of rain, even distant, don't enter: flash floods are deadly in these narrows.

If you have a high-clearance vehicle, push on to Moonscape Overlook, 30 minutes from Hanksville. This viewpoint looks over a valley of undulating gray hills that resemble the Moon's surface. The best time: at sunset, when the valley takes on silver hues. Photos never do the place justice.

Utah Canyon Loop: Capitol Reef & Goblin Valley

visits.text: You walk to Last Stand Hill at Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, and the white marble headstones stop you flat. On June 25-26, 1876, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors defeated the U.S. Army's 7th Cavalry - 263 soldiers killed out of 650, including Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer and all 209 men under his direct command. The site was renamed from Custer Battlefield by President George H.W. Bush in 1991; red granite markers now stand for fallen Native warriors alongside the white cavalry stones. A 4.5-mile self-guided tour road connects the Custer battlefield to the Reno-Benteen entrenchment where 350 soldiers survived. Paid entry.

Walk through Custer National Cemetery, adjoining the battlefield visitor center. It holds more than 5,000 veterans with interments from the Indian Wars era through the Korean War, and began as a repository for remains collected from abandoned frontier military posts across the region. The grave markers and the surrounding silence of the Montana prairie create a stark contrast with the battlefield just over the hill. Free access, included with battlefield entry.

Take the Deep Ravine Trail to understand the terrain the battle was actually fought on. The path follows the ridge where Custer's battalion made its final movements before collapse, and the dry grasses and rolling bluffs look much as they did in 1876. Don't miss the Indian Memorial on Last Stand Hill - a circular stone structure dedicated on June 25, 2003, the first formal acknowledgment of the Native American perspective built into the monument itself. Allow at least 30 minutes for this walk on top of the main visit.

activities.text: If you're visiting in late June, make time for the Real Bird family's annual Battle of the Little Bighorn Reenactment at Medicine Tail Coulee near Garryowen - on the actual ground where Custer's battalion was closest to the Native village. Run entirely by Crow tribal members since 1992, it tells the battle from an Indigenous perspective with roughly 170 horses and scenes depicting Sitting Bull's prophecy. Jim Real Bird created the event specifically because, as he put it, 'at the other place, the Indians were invisible.' The 34th edition runs June 26-28, 2026, marking the 150th anniversary. Fee per vehicle.

Drive down to Garryowen and stop at the Custer Battlefield Museum, a private collection at the historic Reno-Benteen site holding what its operators describe as the largest Custer and Sitting Bull collection in the world. It sits directly on the battlefield and takes a more personal, artifact-focused approach than the NPS visitor center - uniforms, personal items, photographs. Take exit 514 off I-90. Pair this with a walk along the Little Bighorn River at dusk, where the cottonwood groves look much as they did when the Lakota encampment stretched for miles along this bank. Small paid admission.

days_plan.itin_title: Montana East: Big Sky Country from Billings to Bismarck

visits.text: You're entering one of the most history-laden towns on the entire East Coast. Harpers Ferry is famous for John Brown's raid in October 1859: this radical abolitionist seized the federal arsenal with 21 men hoping to spark a slave uprising. The town changed hands eight times during the Civil War, and its Victorian Lower Town has remained virtually intact since 1865. Start early to visit before the school buses arrive, and don't miss the view from Jefferson Rock - Thomas Jefferson himself wrote in 1783 that this panorama of the confluence of two rivers was worth 'a voyage across the Atlantic.'

You're standing before this small red brick building - the only remaining vestige of the 1859 raid still standing. John Brown and his men held out here for 36 hours before being captured by Marines commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee - the same man who would lead the Confederate army two years later. The irony of history: the fort was dismantled stone by stone and rebuilt three times in three different locations before returning in 1968 to its original site, within a few meters. The adjacent museum traces the context of the abolitionist movement with documents and testimonies from Brown's contemporaries.

You're standing on the point of land where the Shenandoah meets the Potomac - two rivers with slightly different hues that blend only gradually over several hundred meters. This place already fascinated Lenape tribes long before Europeans arrived, and it was the first natural site on the continent described as 'sublime' by an American president, namely Jefferson. To the north, the 1894 truss railroad bridge crosses both rivers in a single span. In autumn, the red and orange leaves make this viewpoint one of the most photographed images in the entire region.

activities.text: You're climbing through forest for 45 minutes on a rocky trail, then the vegetation opens onto the ruins of Confederate artillery batteries from 1862. At the summit - 448 meters - the complete panorama unfolds below: Lower Town, both rivers, the railroad bridges, and the Virginia hills stretching to the horizon. It was from this very spot that Confederate General 'Stonewall' Jackson's army observed the town before taking it in September 1862. Arrive in late afternoon for golden light on the village rooftops.

You're launching onto the Shenandoah just upstream from Harpers Ferry: a few beginner-friendly rapids, banks lined with giant sycamores and weeping willows, and the awareness that you're paddling on a river that Confederate and Union soldiers forded multiple times between 1861 and 1865, sometimes under fire. The view of Loudoun Heights cliffs from the kayak is one of the most spectacular in the region. River Riders and Harpers Ferry Adventure Center offer rentals with shuttle included.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

visits.text: Mark Twain House & Museum - Where American Literature Was Born: Tour the stunning Gothic-style mansion where Samuel Clemens penned 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn,' 'The Adventures of Tom Sawyer,' and other American classics. The elaborately decorated 25-room house, described by Twain as 'part steamboat, part cathedral,' reveals the author's creative genius and domestic life.

Harriet Beecher Stowe Center - The Home That Changed a Nation: Adjacent to the Twain House, this historic site honors the author of 'Uncle Tom's Cabin,' the novel Abraham Lincoln credited with helping start the Civil War. The center continues Stowe's legacy of literary activism.

Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art - America's Oldest Continuously Operating Public Art Museum: Founded in 1842, this castle-like institution houses over 50,000 works spanning 5,000 years across European, American, and contemporary collections. The stunning and diverse holdings rival those of major metropolitan museums.

Old State House - Where Democracy Took Root: This National Historic Landmark served as Connecticut's center of government from 1796 to 1878 and witnessed pivotal moments in American history. Now a museum, it preserves the chambers where early Americans debated the nature of liberty.

Connecticut Science Center - Interactive Discovery on the Riverfront: This striking modern facility overlooking the Connecticut River features hundreds of hands-on exhibits exploring everything from outer space to the human body, with a state-of-the-art planetarium and 3D theater.

activities.text: Bushnell Center for Performing Arts - New England's Premier Performance Venue: This historic theater hosts Broadway tours, world-class concerts, and cultural events in an ornate setting that has entertained Hartford audiences since 1930.

Connecticut Art Trail - 250 Miles, 21 Institutions, 500,000 Works: This statewide route showcases Connecticut's pivotal role in American Impressionism through museums from Greenwich to Hartford, including entry to the Wadsworth Atheneum and numerous specialized collections.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Coastal Drive: From Maritime Mystic to Ivy League New Haven

places.name: Hattiesburg, MS

visits.text: One of the only museums in the world dedicated solely to African American military history is found here—installed in a 1942 USO Club reserved for Black soldiers (segregation mandated). Six wars covered, from the Civil War to Iraq. Entire room on the Tuskegee Airmen, African American pilots who flew 1,491 missions without losing a single escorted bomber in Europe. Free admission, open Tuesday-Saturday.

Quirky and unexpected, the Hattiesburg Pocket Museum is a 3-foot-wide "museum" in a niche between two buildings on Front Street—miniature exhibitions changed monthly (Barbie dolls, Cold War objects, outsider art miniatures). Free, open 24/7. All around, the historic downtown features over 70 murals since 2014, a municipal program that revitalized the former railroad district.

Nine miles south, Camp Shelby is the largest National Guard training base in the United States, active since 1917—and its military museum is one of the South's largest. Exceptional exhibition on the 442nd Infantry Regiment, the most decorated Japanese American unit in U.S. military history, trained here in 1943 while the soldiers' families were in internment camps. Free admission, ID check at base entrance.

activities.text: You bike the Longleaf Trace—a 41-mile greenway built on a former railroad line, connecting Hattiesburg to Prentiss through longleaf pine forest. Flat, paved, shaded. Rental at Trace Station in Hattiesburg ($15 half-day). The urban section is also walkable without renting.

visits.text: Chateau Montelena, Calistoga: the other winner of the 1976 Judgment of Paris, white category. The 1973 Chardonnay vinified by Mike Grgich - a Croat who would later found his own winery, Grgich Hills - beat Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet blind before a French jury. The stone château was built in 1888 by Alfred Tubbs, a merchant who studied viticulture in Bordeaux. The 1970s restoration by Jim Barrett returned it to its original appearance. Today's Estate Chardonnay is the direct descendant of the 1973. Reservation required.

Old Faithful Geyser of California, Calistoga: one of three 'faithful' geysers in the world (along with Yellowstone and one in New Zealand). It erupts every 10 to 30 minutes depending on underground pressure, up to 20 meters high, water at 78°C. Not grandiose in the Yellowstone sense, but the punctuality of the phenomenon is real - unlike many geysers that fall off schedule. $15, 30 minutes is enough.

Healdsburg Plaza, arrival point in Sonoma: a town of 12,000 organized around a palm-planted central square, with about fifty tasting rooms within walking distance. The contrast with Napa is immediate - less marble, more wood, fewer $100 labels, more winemakers serving themselves. Healdsburg SHED (25 North Street) is Sonoma Wine Country's reference gourmet grocery.

Williams-Selyem, 10701 Westside Road: founded in 1979 by Burt Williams and Ed Selyem in a Fulton garage, this winery became the cult reference for American Pinot Noir. Their 2007 Litton Estate received 100/100 in Wine Spectator in 2009 - the first North American Pinot to reach that score in a major magazine. Problem: visits are reserved for mailing list members, and the waiting list extends several years. If you get access: it's a real opportunity. Otherwise, Gary Farrell Vineyards right next door (10701 Westside Road as well, separate entrance) offers a plunging view of Russian River Valley from its tasting room.

Iron Horse Vineyards, Sebastopol: 25 minutes west of Healdsburg, on the edge of the Sonoma Coast. The estate founded in 1979 produces Méthode Champenoise served at the White House since Ronald Reagan - every president since has continued the tradition. The tasting happens outdoors on a terrace with 360° views of the vines. This isn't a drive-by winery: the detour from Healdsburg is worth it for the landscape contrast and the very different style from Russian River reds.

activities.text: Crossing the Mayacamas Mountains via Highway 128: 1 hour of switchbacks between Calistoga and Healdsburg, through the range separating Napa from Sonoma. The road is narrow, the turns tight, and the views of both valleys are worth the effort. This isn't a road to be in a hurry on - that's exactly why it deserves to be savored.

First glass of Sonoma Pinot noir in Healdsburg: The Matheson (106 Matheson Street) is the Plaza's reference restaurant-bar, with an impressive cellar of local wines by the glass. It's the right way to enter Sonoma County: mentally compare with the Cabernets of the last three days. The difference is immediate - less body, more fruit, marked acidity.

Westside Road drive: Sonoma County's most beautiful wine road. You follow the Russian River between Healdsburg and Guerneville for about twenty kilometers, under eucalyptus and redwoods. The sandy Goldridge soils - the secret of the valley's great Pinots - are visible in the roadside terrain cuts. Drive slowly, without agenda.

Winemaker's picnic between tastings: buy bread, cheeses, and charcuterie at Big John's Market in Healdsburg (1345 Healdsburg Avenue), add a bottle of Pinot bought that morning, and find a table corner in the gardens of one of the wineries that allows it (Gary Farrell, notably). It's cheaper than a starred restaurant and often better than you expect.

places.name: Healy, AK

visits.text: Take the Parks Highway south from Fairbanks about 100 miles to Denali Park entrance, via Healy. Don't rush the drive - on your right shortly past Nenana, the Nenana River canyon opens suddenly: the glacial river carves a gorge through rock for several miles, turquoise waters contrasting against dark walls. Outfitters offer rafting trips on these waters from Denali Park village, just at the park entrance. At the Denali Visitor Center, pick up your maps, check current weather and Park Road conditions - Denali (20,310 feet) is visible only 30% of the time from the entrance area.

The entire day is devoted to the park transit bus - reserve your seat at reservedenali.com, as spots fill quickly in July-August. In 2026, buses run to mile 43 (East Fork River) due to construction at the Pretty Rocks slide. Green transit buses are hop-on/hop-off: you get off wherever you want on the road, then catch any following green bus. The road winds through open tundra - from the bus you'll watch for grizzlies (300 to 350 individuals in the park's north section), caribou herds (about 1,500 in the Denali herd), Dall sheep clinging to white ridges, and perhaps a wolf. Bring binoculars - wildlife is often distant. On clear days, Stony Hill Overlook (mile 62, inaccessible this year but visible from accessible areas) and surrounding ridges offer direct views of Denali.

Start the morning at the park's sled dog kennels - take the Kennels Shuttle from the Visitor Center. Demonstrations run at 10am, 2pm, and 4pm in high season (June-September) and last 30 minutes. This program began in 1922 when the park's first superintendent, Harry Karstens, bought the first 7 dogs for $45 each to patrol the wilderness. Today, about thirty dogs live and work here - the only active kennel in the entire National Park Service. You can pet most of the dogs in the dog yard between demonstrations.

Drive to Savage River (mile 15) - it's the end of the road accessible by private vehicle. Arrive early, as parking is limited. The Savage River Loop Trail is 3 miles flat along the river, with a crossing bridge: on the slopes above, scan for Dall sheep with binoculars - about 2,500 individuals inhabit the park. The transition from boreal forest to open tundra happens right in this zone, making it one of the best places at the entrance to grasp Denali's signature landscape.

activities.text: Early afternoon, take the free Riley Creek Loop shuttle from the Visitor Center - it serves Riley Creek Campground, the Bus Depot, and the Horseshoe Lake trailhead. The Horseshoe Lake Trail is 1.5 miles round-trip from the bus stop: the descent through spruce forest leads to a horseshoe-shaped lake dammed by beavers. It's one of the best spots in the entrance area for moose watching, especially early morning. In the evening, if you arrive before 5pm, catch the sled dog demonstration at the park kennels (2 miles from entrance) - rangers explain a program dating back to 1922, the only active kennel in the entire National Park Service.

Late day after your bus return, hike to Horseshoe Lake trail if you missed it yesterday, or try the Mount Healy Overlook Trail from the Visitor Center: 5.6 miles round-trip with 1,700 feet elevation gain, it climbs through birch forest then emerges onto an open ridge with views across the entrance valley and, on clear days, Denali's summit on the horizon. Allow 3 hours round-trip and wear good boots - upper slopes can be slippery.

For hikers, the Savage Alpine Trail leaves from the same parking lot: point-to-point climb toward the ridge with sweeping views over the valley. Caution - bears have been reported on this trail, carry bear spray and make noise. Evening, quiet return to Healy: restaurants in the Denali Park Village area serve local dishes. Weather changes very quickly in this zone - always carry extra layers in your pack.

visits.text: Step into the charming Bavarian-themed village of Helen, where colorful Alpine architecture, flower-draped balconies, and cobblestone walkways create an unexpected European atmosphere nestled in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Over 200 specialty shops, authentic German bakeries, and traditional restaurants line the pedestrian-friendly streets beneath forested peaks. The town hosts the longest Oktoberfest celebration in America, spanning two full months of festive activities.

Hike to Anna Ruby Falls, a spectacular dual waterfall where two creeks plunge side by side into a misty pool surrounded by lush mountain forest. The accessible trail winds through hardwood groves and rhododendron thickets, offering a refreshing escape into pristine wilderness just minutes from town. Interpretive displays explain the area's unique ecology.

activities.text: Sample wines at local vineyards producing distinctive Georgia varietals, then browse the Helen Arts & Heritage Center documenting the town's transformation from declining logging community to beloved tourist destination. The Chattahoochee River flows directly through town, perfect for tubing adventures.

visits.text: Atchafalaya Basin - The largest swamp in North America: 600,000 hectares of black water, bald cypress, and Spanish moss. Henderson, a small Cajun village on the levee, is the gateway to the basin. The landscape is otherworldly—cathedrals of cypress rise from dark, still water.

activities.text: Take a boat tour in the Atchafalaya Basin - Several operators depart from Henderson for 1.5- to 2-hour swamp tours. You'll navigate between centuries-old cypress, spotting alligators, turtles, great blue herons, and bald eagles. Early morning and late afternoon are best—the light filtering through the moss is spectacular.

Eat crawfish in Henderson - Levee restaurants in Henderson serve all-you-can-eat boiled crawfish during the season (January–June). You eat them on newspaper, spiced with Cayenne, alongside corn and potatoes. Get messy with your hands—no utensils allowed.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Louisiana Road Trip: Jazz and Bayous

visits.text: Visit the Henderson County Heritage Museum, which provides comprehensive accounts of local history and culture through engaging exhibits and artifacts. The museum offers visitors an excellent introduction to the heritage of this charming mountain foothill community.

Discover the Mineral & Lapidary Museum along Hendersonville's vibrant Main Street, featuring a varied collection of gemstones, minerals, and precious stones found and mined throughout North Carolina. This fascinating museum showcases the geological treasures that lie beneath the Carolina soil.

activities.text: Engage young minds at Hands On! Children's Museum, where interactive exhibits and hands-on activities entertain and educate visitors of all ages. For a change of scenery, escape to the open tranquility of Saint Paul Mountain Vineyards, where you can sample sweet local wines while enjoying stunning mountain views.

visits.text: Day 2 - The High Line beautifully closes the day: 1.45 miles of aerial railway converted into a garden, between wild grasses, artworks, and walkways above Tenth Avenue. Free, open until evening. Count 45 min to 1 hour strolling north to Hudson Yards.

Day 2 - On the High Line, original rails still surface between the perennials planted by Piet Oudolf. Viewpoints follow one another: Hudson Yards' coppery Vessel, the Empire State in the distance, Zaha Hadid's building along the park. Very busy on weekends; weekday mornings it's nearly yours.

activities.text: Possible mid-route exit at 23rd Street for Chelsea's art galleries, free, concentrated between 20th and 27th Streets.
End of Day 2. Toward the Empire State Building for tomorrow morning: 1.6 km from Hudson Yards, on foot via 34th Street or by subway, about 15 min.

places.name: Hilton Head Island, SC

visits.text: Explore Hilton Head Island's pristine beaches, featuring miles of soft, pale sand perfect for cycling, dolphin watching, and spectacular sunrise viewing. The island's coastline transforms into brilliant shades of pink and gold at dawn, creating an atmosphere of tranquility that defines this barrier island paradise. With gentle waves and wide-open stretches, this destination offers quintessential Lowcountry relaxation.

Discover Harbour Town, the island's iconic waterfront village crowned by the distinctive red-and-white striped lighthouse. Climb the lighthouse for panoramic coastal views stretching across the marshlands and harbor. The village combines maritime charm with boutique shopping and waterfront dining in a picturesque setting.

activities.text: Cycle through more than 60 miles of scenic trails shaded by magnificent live oaks draped in Spanish moss. These pathways wind through maritime forests, past lagoons teeming with wildlife, and along beaches where the sand is firm enough for extended rides. The island's extensive trail network makes it one of the most bike-friendly destinations in the Southeast.

Paddle through the calm salt marshes by kayak, gliding past herons, dolphins, and jumping fish in some of the most pristine waterways in the Lowcountry. The Art League Gallery and the Gullah Museum of Hilton Head Island offer cultural enrichment, showcasing regional artistry and the rich heritage of the Gullah people.
