visits.text: Mendenhall Glacier—12 miles from downtown Juneau, accessible by bus or taxi—is the only major glacier in Southeast Alaska accessible by road. The glacier descends from the Juneau Icefield (over 1,500 square miles) and has retreated more than 2 miles since the 1930s. From the Visitor Center platform, the blue face is in direct view above Mendenhall Lake. The trail to Nugget Falls (0.9 miles one-way) follows the shore to the base of the waterfall—one of the most beautiful accessible hikes in Alaska.

The Alaska State Capitol in downtown Juneau is one of the few American capitols without a dome. The building was constructed in 1931 as the Federal and Territorial Building—Alaska wasn't yet a state. It became the seat of state government only after Alaska's admission to the Union in 1959. Free guided tours (45 minutes) show the Senate and House chambers with their Alaska wood inlays, and explain how to govern a 663,000-square-mile state from a capital accessible only by air or sea.

The Last Chance Mining Museum, perched at the end of a narrow road northeast of downtown, occupies the remnants of the Alaska-Juneau mine—one of the world's largest low-grade gold mines at its peak in the 1930s. The steam-powered machinery and partially restored galleries tell how they extracted half an ounce of gold per ton of rock. The admission is modest and the experience worthwhile.

activities.text: Tracy Arm Fjord, 55 miles southeast of Juneau, is one of Alaska's most spectacular fjords—25 miles of rock walls covered in waterfalls leading to the twin Sawyer glaciers. Fast boats depart Juneau harbor in the morning and return late afternoon. The fjord is often choked with blue icebergs in summer—the boat weaves between them, yards from glacier faces that calve regularly.

Humpback whale watching in the Inside Passage channels from Juneau is among Alaska's most reliable in summer. Over 100 individuals frequent these waters from June to September to feed. Charters offer 3- to 4-hour trips from the harbor—bubble-net feeding behavior is regularly observed, something few other spots in the world can offer.

days_plan.itin_title: Alaska Adventure - 14 Days Through the World's Most Remote National Parks

visits.text: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park — Witness ongoing volcanic activity at Kilauea, one of the world's most active volcanoes. The 1,348-square-kilometer park encompasses the summit caldera, lava tubes, steam vents, and barren lava fields from recent eruptions.

Thurston Lava Tube — Walk through this 150-meter tunnel formed 500 years ago when lava drained leaving a hollow tube. Ferns and native plants surround the entrance while the interior reveals smooth walls created by flowing molten rock.

Chain of Craters Road — Drive 30 kilometers descending from summit to sea across vast lava fields. The scenic route passes extinct craters, petroglyphs, and the Holei Sea Arch where lava enters the ocean creating new land.

Jaggar Museum Overlook — View the Kilauea caldera from the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory perched on the crater rim. When active, the lava lake glows orange against night skies while sulfur dioxide plumes rise from the summit.

Mauna Kea Summit — Ascend to 4,207 meters atop Hawaii's tallest mountain for sunset and stargazing from the world's premier astronomical observation site. Thirteen international telescopes crown the dormant volcano rising 10,200 meters from seafloor to summit.

Akaka Falls State Park — Hike the 0.6-kilometer loop trail through bamboo groves and rainforest to viewpoints of 135-meter Akaka Falls. The free-falling plunge pool empties into a lush gorge while 30-meter Kahuna Falls cascades nearby.

Rainbow Falls — Photograph this 24-meter waterfall best viewed in morning light when rainbows form in the mist. Located in Hilo, the cascade plunges over a lava cave where legend says Hawaiian goddess Hina lives.

Puuhonua o Honaunau National Historical Park — Explore this reconstructed Hawaiian place of refuge where kapu breakers and defeated warriors found sanctuary. The 73-hectare park preserves royal grounds, fishponds, and the Great Wall built around 1550.

activities.text: Black sand beach at Punaluu — Walk across volcanic sand formed by lava shattering on contact with cold ocean water. Endangered green sea turtles bask on the black beach beneath coconut palms in this remote South Point location.

Kona coffee farm tour — Learn how 100% Kona coffee grows on the volcanic slopes of Hualalai and Mauna Loa. Family farms offer tours explaining cultivation, harvesting, and roasting of this premium Hawaiian coffee variety.

Historic Kailua-Kona waterfront — Stroll past Hulihe'e Palace and Mokuaikaua Church, Hawaii's oldest Christian church built in 1820. The oceanfront village served as King Kamehameha I's royal compound from 1812 until his 1819 death.

Manta ray night snorkel — Swim with graceful manta rays attracted to plankton illuminated by underwater lights off Kona coast. The 4-meter wingspan giants glide inches from snorkelers in an unforgettable marine encounter.

Green sand beach hike — Trek 4.8 kilometers to Papakolea Beach, one of only four green sand beaches worldwide. Olivine crystals eroding from the cinder cone create the distinctive olive-colored sand accessible only by foot.

Fresh poke bowl dinner — Sample cubed raw fish marinated in soy sauce, sesame oil, and limu seaweed at local markets or restaurants. This Hawaiian staple showcases the islands' Pacific Rim culinary influences.

places.name: Kalamazoo, MI

visits.text: You drive through Battle Creek and understand why this city of 52,000 calls itself 'Cereal City USA': this is where Dr. John Harvey Kellogg, a Seventh-day Adventist physician, invented corn flakes in 1894 while seeking healthy food for his sanitarium patients. His brother Will Keith Kellogg founded the Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company here in 1906 - today Kellogg's, one of the world's largest food corporations. Charles William Post, a former sanitarium patient, copied the idea and founded Post Cereals in the same city in 1895. For decades, the smell of toasted grains floated over the entire town. The Kellogg's Discovery Center traces this history with interactive installations on nutrition, industrial heritage, and American breakfast culture. Allow 2 hours on-site. Open Tuesday-Saturday 10am-5pm, admission $8 adult.

You arrive at the Gilmore Car Museum in Hickory Corners, between Battle Creek and Kalamazoo, and find 90 acres of prairie dotted with historic barns filled with 400 vehicles spanning 130 years of American automotive history - the Midwest's largest open-air collection. Founded in 1966 by Donald Gilmore, heir to a Michigan pharmaceutical fortune, the museum gathers rarities like the first series-production Ford Mustang (1964), 1920s Packards, a 1942 Lincoln Continental, and dozens of racing cars. The architecture of restored 19th-century barns housing the collections gives the place a particularly successful atmosphere: you pass from barn to barn as through a village. Open daily May through October, 9am-5pm; admission $15 adult. Reserve at least 2 hours.

You enter Bell's Brewery's Eccentric Café in Kalamazoo and you're standing in one of the most influential breweries in American craft beer history. Larry Bell opened his first brewery in 1985 in a converted soup kitchen, with a 15-gallon kettle and a detergent pump for hops - making it one of the very first microbreweries in the Midwest. Their Two Hearted Ale, an IPA with pine and grapefruit aromas named after a Michigan river dear to Hemingway, was voted best beer in America by the American Homebrewers Association in 2017. The Eccentric Café, their historic pub, still offers the full range on tap with pub fare in a brick-and-timber space. Open Monday-Thursday 11am-10pm, Friday-Saturday until 11pm.

activities.text: You explore downtown Kalamazoo on foot between multiple craft breweries - the city was voted Beer City USA two consecutive years in 2012 and 2013, a nationally voted title among beer enthusiasts. Bell's Brewery is the historic reference, but Arcadia Brewing (English-style ales since 1996) and Kalamazoo Beer Exchange (dynamic pricing system based on demand, like a stock exchange) offer complementary experiences in the same walkable downtown district. Kalamazoo is also home to Western Michigan University (23,000 students), giving downtown a particularly lively student atmosphere in the evening.

You enter the Kalamazoo Institute of Arts, a municipal art museum with entirely free admission, and find a permanent collection of 6,000 works spanning 19th-century American art to the present. The museum also organizes public art classes and temporary exhibitions that regularly attract nationally recognized contemporary artists. The building itself, renovated in 2012, integrates naturally lit spaces that highlight collection pieces. A 45-minute break here contrasts nicely with the industrial day between Kellogg's and the Gilmore Car Museum.

places.name: Kanab, UT

visits.text: Kanab bills itself as "Little Hollywood"—over 100 films and TV shows were shot in its surroundings, from John Wayne westerns to Planet of the Apes. The town of 5,000 is a strategic crossroads between Zion, Bryce, Grand Canyon, and Lake Powell. Take a stroll through downtown—the Western storefronts are authentic, not sets.

Twenty minutes south, Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park is a field of pink sand dunes—Utah's only one. The dunes rise up to 100 feet high. You can walk on them, slide, or simply contemplate the contrast between pink sand and surrounding red cliffs.

activities.text: Kanab is also the gateway to The Wave (Coyote Buttes North), the Southwest's most famous sandstone formation—but permits are awarded by lottery and very limited (64 per day). If you don't have a permit, White Pocket in the Vermilion Cliffs offers equally spectacular rock formations—you need a 4x4 and GPS, but no permit.

places.name: Kansas, KS

visits.text: Walk across the glass bridge at the National WWI Museum and look down — beneath your feet are 9,000 red poppies, each representing 1,000 combatant deaths. This is America's only federally designated WWI museum, built beneath the 217-foot Liberty Memorial tower that Kansas City erected after 83,000 citizens raised $2.5 million in just ten days in 1919. The 1921 site dedication was the only time the supreme commanders of all five Allied nations stood in the same place. From the tower's observation deck you get the best panorama in Kansas City. Budget two hours for the museum plus the tower. Paid entry; the Over There Café is open without a ticket.

The Arabia Steamboat Museum in the City Market is running its final year — the Hawley family announced closing in November 2026 after 35 years, so this visit has a deadline. On September 5, 1856, the 171-foot steamboat Arabia hit a tree snag and sank 6 miles west of Kansas City, carrying 200 tons of cargo bound for 16 frontier towns. The Missouri River shifted course, and the Arabia lay buried 45 feet underground beneath a Kansas cornfield for 132 years until treasure hunters dug it up in 1988. The collection is the largest single assemblage of pre-Civil War artifacts in the world. Allow 90 minutes.

Four badminton shuttlecocks, each 18 feet tall and weighing 5,500 pounds, sit on the lawn of the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art as if giants had just abandoned a game. Artists Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen installed them in July 1994, using the neoclassical building as a net and the 22-acre lawn as the court. The museum itself holds one of the country's great encyclopedic collections — standout rooms include the ancient Chinese galleries, a Caravaggio, and the photography wing. Free admission; free outdoor access at any hour.

activities.text: Kaw Point Park sits at the confluence of the Kansas and Missouri Rivers on the east side of Kansas City, and a short interpretive loop tells the story of Lewis and Clark's camp here on June 26, 1804. Ten minutes from downtown, often overlooked, and worth the detour — standing at the exact meeting point of the two rivers connects Day 4 directly back to the Corps. The park is small, the trail is under a mile, and the industrial backdrop makes the historical fact feel even starker.

The City Market district surrounding the Arabia Steamboat Museum has operated as a public market since 1857. On weekends, the outdoor farmers' market draws crowds to stalls selling Missouri produce, local charcuterie, and every kind of food. Kansas City smoked meat culture is distinct enough that a meal here qualifies as cultural research — the tradition of low-and-slow hickory-smoked brisket, burnt ends, and ribs runs through dozens of family-owned joints within a few miles of downtown.

visits.text: From Bluff, take US-163 south. About 10 miles from Monument Valley, the road opens onto the Southwest's most famous view—the straight line of asphalt shooting toward the Mittens. This is the exact spot where Forrest Gump stops running in the film. Pull over on the shoulder for the photo.

Monument Valley isn't a national park—it's a Tribal Park managed by the Navajo Nation. The sandstone buttes rise up to 1,000 feet above the desert floor. The Valley Drive is a 17-mile dirt road with 11 numbered stops. You can drive it yourself (allow 2 hours with stops), but the track is rough in places—a high-clearance vehicle is preferable. The Mittens (East and West) and Merrick Butte are the three most photographed formations. According to Navajo legend, these are a giant's hands scattered after a great battle.

The Wildcat Trail is the park's only unguided hike—a 3.2-mile loop around West Mitten Butte. Allow 2 hours. You see the butte from every angle, up close, with desert silence all around. Everything else in the park (Mystery Valley, Hunts Mesa, petroglyphs) requires a Navajo guide—outfitters offer Jeep tours from the visitor center.

activities.text: Don't miss sunrise and sunset at Monument Valley. The buttes change color in minutes—from deep red to purple. From the visitor center parking lot, the panoramic view of the Mittens at sunset is free and accessible without entering the park. At night, zero light pollution—the Milky Way is spectacular.

visits.text: The Sun Valley Lodge opened on December 21, 1936, built in seven months on the former 3,888-acre Brass Ranch for $1.5 million by Union Pacific Railroad chairman Averell Harriman - who also installed the world's first chairlift here, designed by engineer Jim Curran using banana-loading conveyor technology from tropical cargo ships. The four-story, X-shaped building looks today exactly as it did then: concrete poured inside rough-sawn forms and acid-stained to resemble wood. Walk the hallways - they're lined with black-and-white photographs of Clark Gable, Ingrid Bergman, and Marilyn Monroe. In suite 206, Hemingway finished writing For Whom the Bell Tolls in the fall of 1939.

About 1.5 miles northeast of the Lodge on Trail Creek Road, a bronze bust by sculptor Robert Berks marks the Hemingway Memorial. It was dedicated on July 21, 1966 - his birthday, five years after his death in nearby Ketchum. The inscription is a eulogy Hemingway himself wrote in 1939 for a friend killed in a hunting accident, ending: 'Now he will be part of them forever.' The road closes in deep winter. Trail Creek itself runs below the memorial, clear enough to see the bottom.

On North Main Street, Hemingway's grave in the Ketchum Cemetery sits between two large spruce trees under a flat granite slab - usually decorated with bottles of whiskey left by visitors. He moved to Ketchum permanently in 1959 and died here on July 2, 1961. Nearby, the free Wood River Museum of History and Culture (4th and Walnut, Tuesday-Saturday 11 AM-6 PM) has an exhibit with original artifacts and a vintage typewriter you can use. The museum also covers Sun Valley's ski history and the local mining era.

activities.text: The Pioneer Cabin Trail climbs 4.5 miles west of Ketchum to a stone cabin at 9,400 feet, built by Union Pacific in 1937 as a ski hut. Three thousand feet of elevation gain, mostly in the first two miles through shaded pine - the hard part is done early. From the ridge, the Pioneer Mountains open up in every direction. Allow 5-6 hours round trip; late June through September for best conditions. Dogs welcome off-leash.

The Pioneer Saloon on Main Street has been here since Hemingway's era and still displays one of his personal shotguns - a 1953 Winchester Model 21 he used bird hunting on nearby Silver Creek. The Ram restaurant opened in 1938 and is the oldest at the resort. For the full literary cocktail experience, the Sawtooth Club serves the original Hemingway daiquiri recipe brought back from the El Floridita bar in Havana.

places.name: Key Largo, FL

visits.text: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park - America's first underwater park, established in 1963. It encompasses 92 square miles of Atlantic Ocean along Key Largo. The visitor center houses a 30,000-gallon saltwater aquarium - a solid preview of the reef if you're not diving. Cannon Beach and Far Beach are the park's two beaches, small but peaceful. Arrive early in the morning - weekend parking fills up fast.

Dagny Johnson Key Largo Hammock Botanical State Park - This park protects one of the last remaining West Indian tropical hardwood hammock forests in the Keys. The main trail (1.5 km round trip) winds through a dense canopy of gumbo-limbo and mahogany trees. You might spot the Key Largo woodrat, an endangered species found only on this island.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Christ of the Abyss - Key Largo's most iconic excursion. This 8.5-foot bronze statue, submerged 25 feet deep near Dry Rocks, is a replica of the 1954 original placed off Genoa, Italy. Operators within Pennekamp park offer 2.5-hour boat trips - the statue's crown sits 6-10 feet below the surface, easily visible while snorkeling. Book the day before or morning of your visit.

Kayaking through Key Largo's mangroves - Outfitters offer guided trips through sheltered mangrove channels, protected from wind. The water runs shallow and crystal-clear - you'll see rays, juvenile lemon sharks, and herons. Best in late afternoon when the heat eases off.

places.name: Key West, FL

visits.text: Seven Mile Bridge - The most memorable stretch of the Overseas Highway. This 6.8-mile bridge (not seven miles, but the name stuck) connects Marathon to the Lower Keys above strikingly clear turquoise water. Alongside it, the 1912 railroad bridge, partially demolished, remains visible - its broken arches give the landscape a post-apocalyptic edge. No stopping on the bridge itself, but you can pull over at either end for photos.

Bahia Honda State Park - Often ranked among America's most beautiful beaches. The sand is fine, the water clear and shallow for dozens of yards. Three beaches to choose from: Sandspur Beach (the largest), Calusa Beach (facing the old bridge), and Loggerhead Beach (more secluded). The park has limited capacity - arrive before 10am in high season or you'll find the gates closed.

National Key Deer Refuge on Big Pine Key - These miniature Key deer (24-30 inches at the shoulder) live only in the Lower Keys. The population numbers around 700-800. The best viewing spot is the Blue Hole, a former quarry pit filled with fresh water where alligators coexist with the deer. Drive slowly on Big Pine Key - speed limits are reduced to protect the deer.

Ernest Hemingway Home & Museum - The 1851 colonial mansion where Hemingway lived from 1931 to 1939. This is where he wrote 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' and 'The Snows of Kilimanjaro.' The real stars are the 50-60 cats ruling the property - about half are polydactyl (six-toed), descendants of Snow White, a cat given to Hemingway by a ship's captain. The 30-minute guided tour (included with admission) also covers the $20,000 pool from 1937, the penny embedded in the ground, and the bar urinal converted into a fountain by his ex-wife.

Southernmost Point - The famous concrete buoy marking the southernmost point in the continental United States (24°33'N), 90 miles from Cuba. Lines form almost constantly for the photo - early morning or late afternoon is calmer.

Fort Zachary Taylor State Park - The best swimming and snorkeling spot in Key West proper. The brick fort (1845-1866) served as a naval base during the Civil War. The beach is rocky (bring water shoes) but tropical fish swarm a few yards from shore. The trees provide shade, rare in Key West.

Key West Cemetery - This 1847 cemetery, right in the middle of town, is one of Florida's strangest. Graves are above-ground (the water table sits 12 inches down). Some epitaphs are deliberately comic - the most famous reads 'I told you I was sick.' A 30-minute wander is plenty.

Dry Tortugas National Park - Fort Jefferson - Full day devoted to this excursion 70 miles west of Key West. The ferry departs at 8am and returns around 5:30pm (2 hours 15 minutes each way). Fort Jefferson is a massive red brick hexagon planted on Garden Key - one of the largest coastal forts ever built in the United States, with walls 8 feet thick. Construction began in 1846 and was never completed. During the Civil War it served as a prison - the most famous inmate was Dr. Samuel Mudd, convicted for setting the broken leg of John Wilkes Booth after Lincoln's assassination. The guided fort tour runs 45 minutes.

Duval Street and Old Town - Key West's main drag, 1.25 miles between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic. Morning, before the cruise ship crowds arrive, is the best time to wander among Victorian wooden houses, art galleries, and cafes. At the street's end, Mile Marker 0 marks the beginning (or end) of US Route 1, which stretches from Key West to the Canadian border in Maine - 2,369 miles.

Custom House Museum - This red brick 1891 building, formerly the port customs house, now houses a local art and history museum. Exhibits cover wrecking (salvaging shipwrecks, Key West's main industry in the 19th century), cigar manufacturing, and military history. Handsome Richardson Romanesque architecture.

Key West Butterfly and Nature Conservatory - A 5,000-square-foot tropical greenhouse housing 50-60 butterfly species in free flight, plus flamingos and tropical birds. Restful after days in full sun - the interior is shaded and humid.

activities.text: Swimming and lounging at Bahia Honda - Take your time here. The water is the most beautiful in the Keys - turquoise, warm, calm. If you have mask and snorkel, the snorkeling from the beach is decent, with scattered coral and tropical fish. In late afternoon, the low sun casts golden tones across the sand.

Sunset at Mallory Square - Every evening, two hours before sunset, the square transforms into an impromptu festival: jugglers, fire-breathers, musicians, street vendors. Everyone gathers facing west to watch the sun drop into the Gulf of Mexico. Arrive early for a good spot.

Snorkeling at Dry Tortugas - The water around Fort Jefferson is exceptionally clear (50-100 foot visibility) and depths range from 5 to 15 feet. Snorkeling gear is included with the ferry ticket. You'll see barracuda, sea turtles, grouper, and intact coral formations - this is some of Florida's finest snorkeling. Pack waterproof sunscreen - there's almost no shade on the island.

Key lime pie tasting - The Keys' signature lime pie is THE local dessert. The original recipe uses Key West limes (smaller and more tart than standard limes), sweetened condensed milk, and a Graham cracker crust. Sample several versions for comparison - every establishment has their take. The frozen-on-a-stick version dipped in chocolate is a street classic.

Final sunset or departure - If driving back to Miami (160 miles, 3.5-4 hours), leave in early afternoon to avoid night driving on the Overseas Highway. Otherwise, Key West airport offers direct flights to Miami, Fort Lauderdale, and other Florida cities.

visits.text: Experience the pristine natural beauty of Kiawah Island, where endless stretches of soft sand meet towering dunes and lush maritime forests untouched by commercial development. Sunlight filters through ancient trees in the most captivating ways, while deer, herons, and dolphins appear regularly throughout the landscape. This barrier island represents coastal South Carolina at its most refined.

Cycle along miles of shaded pathways winding through forests, past lagoons filled with wildlife, and directly onto beaches where firm sand allows extended rides along the shore. The island's world-famous golf courses, including the Ocean Course with its dramatic oceanfront holes, attract players from around the globe seeking championship-caliber challenges amid stunning scenery.

activities.text: Paddle through Kiawah's salt marshes at sunset when the landscape transforms into golden hues reflected across calm waters. Beach days reveal why this island consistently ranks among America's finest, with uncrowded shores and crystal-clear waters. The quiet luxury and naturally wild character create an atmosphere of peaceful exclusivity.

places.name: Kingman, AZ

visits.text: Seligman - Stop here - this is where Route 66 was saved. In 1987, Angel Delgadillo, a local barber, founded the Route 66 Association of Arizona to prevent the Mother Road from fading into obscurity after its decommissioning. The few-block village inspired Radiator Springs in the movie Cars. The Snow Cap Drive-In, founded by Angel's brother in 1953, is a temple of kitsch with gags on the menu ('dead chicken' for chicken) and squirting mustard.

Seligman - Kingman: the most beautiful stretch - The 90 miles between these two towns is the best-preserved section of all of Route 66. Two lanes, no traffic, the same road as in 1955 through sagebrush and ranches. Take your time.

Hackberry General Store - Make the stop 30 miles east of Kingman - this 1930s former gas station is frozen in time: period pumps, rusted signs, red Corvette parked out front. It's as authentic as Route 66 gets.

activities.text: Kingman neon lights - If you arrive after dark, Andy Devine Avenue (the local Route 66) lights up with vintage neon. Kingman is also the gateway to the Historic Route 66 toward Oatman - a winding mountain road with wild burros on the pavement.

places.name: Knoxville

visits.text: Market Square has been Knoxville's beating heart since 1854 - when two donors deeded the land to the city, their only condition was that it remain a public market forever. The American Planning Association ranked it among America's best public spaces. Some of the surrounding buildings date back to the 1860s. Linger here for dinner: the outdoor tables stay lively late into the evening.

The Sunsphere Tower rises 266 feet in World's Fair Park - a remnant of the 1982 World's Fair. Go up to the observation deck: the view over Tennessee's wooded hills and Knoxville's skyline is especially beautiful in late afternoon. Admission is free.

activities.text: If you're here on a Saturday between May and November, the Farmers' Market at Market Square opens at 9am. Local producers from eastern Tennessee: cheeses, honey, sourdough breads, charcuterie. It's the best way to see local Knoxville life rather than just passing through.

places.name: Kotzebue, AK

visits.text: The Northwest Arctic Heritage Center in Kotzebue serves as the Visitor Center for three national parks and several monuments—Kobuk Valley, Cape Krusenstern, and Bering Land Bridge. The building itself is a fine museum of Inupiat cultures of northwest Alaska: marine mammal hunting, dog sledding, traditional sewing. Kotzebue is an Inupiat town of 3,000 residents on the Chukchi Sea—one of Alaska's largest Indigenous communities.

Onion Portage in eastern Kobuk Valley National Park (accessible by air from Kotzebue) is one of Alaska's most important archaeological sites: nine different human cultures have succeeded each other here over 12,000 years, all drawn to the same caribou river crossing. The tradition of caribou hunting at this weir location continues today among the Inupiat. Protected site—access through ranger or licensed local guide.

activities.text: Bush plane flight from Kotzebue to the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes—the largest active dunes in the Arctic, 25 square miles of sand 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle. Summer temperatures climb to 100°F on the sand—an absolute paradox in this context. NASA conducted analog studies here to prepare for Mars missions. In summer, wolf, grizzly, and moose tracks crisscross the sand between patches of spruce.

Floating the Kobuk River by packraft or folding canoe—several Kotzebue operators arrange plane drop-offs upriver, with pickup one or two days later. The river flows through boreal forests and Arctic prairies at a gentle pace, mostly Class I. The permafrost bluffs (up to 150 feet) lining the river contain mammoth and steppe bison fossils visible from the boat.

places.name: Lafayette

visits.text: Welcome to Lafayette, heart of Acadiana and self-proclaimed "Happiest City in America." This morning, head to Vermilionville, a living history museum village on the banks of Bayou Vermilion. This site recreates Acadian life from 1765 to 1890 through 19 restored buildings. Period-costumed artisans demonstrate weaving, wood carving, and Cajun cooking. The on-site restaurant, La Cuisine de Maman, serves gumbo and crawfish étouffée prepared according to traditional recipes.

The Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist, downtown, dates from 1916, and its centuries-old oak on the front lawn (the Cathedral Oak, estimated at over 500 years) is one of Louisiana's most photographed trees. The adjacent cemetery, with its above-ground tombs, recalls those of New Orleans.

Explore downtown Lafayette on foot: Jefferson Street concentrates Cajun craft shops, galleries, and colorful murals. The Acadiana Center for the Arts schedules exhibitions and concerts year-round. Lafayette has more restaurants per capita than most American cities—you'll eat well at every meal.

Day trip heading south: drive to Avery Island (50 minutes from Lafayette), birthplace of Tabasco sauce. The McIlhenny family has produced the famous hot sauce here since 1868—same recipe, same place, five generations. Peppers are grown on the island, crushed with local salt, then aged three years in oak barrels (the same ones used for bourbon). The factory tour shows you the entire process, and the shop offers varieties unavailable elsewhere.

Don't leave without exploring Jungle Gardens, 170 acres of botanical gardens and wildlife sanctuary on Avery Island. The garden was created by Edward Avery McIlhenny in the early 20th century. You'll see Bird City, a nesting colony of snowy egrets he saved from extinction in 1895 by raising 8 young birds. Today, thousands of egrets nest there each spring. The park also features a 12th-century Buddha brought from China and an impressive bamboo grove. Warning: signs indicate the presence of black bears—this is not a joke.

On the way back to Lafayette, stop in New Iberia at Shadows-on-the-Teche plantation. This 1834 red-brick mansion, bordered by oaks on the banks of Bayou Teche, is one of the few plantations managed by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Downtown New Iberia also deserves a tour—it's a quiet Cajun town with colorful Creole houses.

activities.text: Evening, look for a Cajun dance or zydeco night. The difference: Cajun music is played on accordion and fiddle, sung in French; zydeco adds the frottoir (washboard) and faster rhythms drawn from blues and R&B. Both are partner dances, with Cajun waltz or two-step. Even if you don't know how to dance, locals will show you—that's the spirit of Acadiana.

Return to Lafayette for dinner. Order a dish you haven't tried yet: boudin (spiced rice and pork sausage, 100% Cajun specialty), gumbo (thick soup based on roux, okra, and seafood or andouille), or crawfish étouffée (crawfish simmered in butter-and-spice sauce).

visits.text: Laguna Beach - Where Art Colony Meets Surf Colony: This Orange County gem has nurtured artists since the early 1900s, with over 100 galleries showcasing works from impressionism to cutting-edge contemporary. World-class waves break just steps away.

Laguna Beach Public Art - Open-Air Museum: The city maintains an impressive collection of outdoor sculptures and murals, from abstract installations on downtown corners to the famous 'Greeter' sculpture welcoming visitors since 1970.

Crystal Cove State Park - 3.2 Miles of Pristine Coastline: This protected stretch preserves undeveloped beachfront between Newport and Laguna, with the charming Historic District of 1930s beach cottages tucked into the bluffs.

Thousand Steps Beach - Worth Every Step: Despite the exaggerated name (it's actually about 230 steps), this steep descent rewards beachgoers with tide pools, sea caves, and some of the finest sand in Orange County.

activities.text: Pageant of the Masters - Living Art Like Nowhere Else: Each summer, this unique festival presents 'living pictures' - real people recreating famous artworks in elaborate tableaux that must be seen to be believed.

visits.text: Haleakala National Park — Sunrise — Ascend to the 3,055-meter summit of this dormant volcano for spectacular sunrise above the clouds. The massive crater spanning 11.2 kilometers houses cinder cones and endemic silversword plants in an otherworldly landscape.

Road to Hana — Navigate 103 kilometers of winding coastal highway featuring 600 curves and 59 bridges through lush rainforest. Waterfalls, black sand beaches, and dramatic ocean views make this one of the world's most scenic drives.

Wailua Falls — Photograph this twin waterfall plunging 24 meters into a tropical pool accessible directly from the road. The cascade appeared in Fantasy Island's opening credits and flows year-round through rainforest vegetation.

Molokini Crater — Snorkel or dive this crescent-shaped volcanic caldera rising from the ocean floor creating a natural aquarium. The partially submerged crater hosts 250 fish species and 38 coral types in crystal-clear waters with 45-meter visibility.

Lahaina Historic District — Explore this former whaling village and Hawaiian royal capital featuring 19th-century buildings and the massive Banyan Tree planted in 1873. The National Historic Landmark preserves missionary homes, the old courthouse, and prison.

Iao Valley State Monument — Hike to viewpoints of the 370-meter Iao Needle, a lava remnant sacred to Hawaiians as Kuka'emoku. The verdant valley receives abundant rainfall creating lush tropical vegetation and was the site of Kamehameha's 1790 battle.

Front Street Lahaina — Browse art galleries, jewelry shops, and restaurants in this oceanfront historic district. The walkable street features whale bones, ship anchors, and maritime heritage from Lahaina's whaling era.

activities.text: Black sand beach at Waianapanapa — Walk across volcanic black pebbles formed by lava meeting ocean creating dramatic contrast against turquoise waters. The state park features lava tubes, sea caves, and ancient Hawaiian burial sites.

Bamboo forest hiking — Trek through dense bamboo groves along the Pipiwai Trail to 122-meter Waimoku Falls. The 6.4-kilometer roundtrip passes banyan trees and traverses boardwalks through magical bamboo cathedral.

Fresh fish plate lunch — Sample ahi poke, loco moco, or teriyaki chicken with rice and macaroni salad at roadside stands. Plate lunch represents Hawaii's multicultural fusion cuisine in generous portions.

Whale watching cruise — Spot humpback whales migrating to Hawaiian waters December through April to mate and calve. The 18-meter mammals breach, tail slap, and sing in the warm Pacific, with up to 10,000 visiting annually.

Sunset dinner cruise — Sail along Maui's west coast enjoying Hawaiian music, tropical cocktails, and buffet dinner as the sun sinks into the Pacific. Catamaran cruises offer romantic evening experiences with whale sightings in season.

visits.text: Discover Lake Allatoona, a sprawling 12,000-acre reservoir surrounded by forested hills and scenic shoreline offering excellent opportunities for swimming, boating, and lakeside relaxation. The clear waters and numerous sandy beaches make this destination perfect for families seeking outdoor recreation combined with natural beauty. Multiple marinas provide boat rentals for exploring hidden coves and peaceful inlets.

Explore the historic Allatoona Pass Battlefield, where dramatic red clay cliffs and a remarkable 175-foot-deep railroad cut tell the story of fierce Civil War combat. The strategic gorge and sweeping views over the lake create a striking landscape where history and natural beauty converge. Walking trails connect key battlefield sites with panoramic overlooks.

activities.text: Hike the Pine Mountain Trail Loop for elevated perspectives over the shimmering lake waters, then camp under starlit skies at Red Top Mountain State Park. The area offers diverse recreational options from fishing and paddleboarding to scenic picnic areas along the forested shoreline.

places.name: Lake City, FL

visits.text: First shock after leaving I-10: Ichetucknee's water runs so clear you can watch turtles breathing ten feet down. Eight springs feed a 6-mile river, designated a National Natural Landmark since 1971. The water emerges from the aquifer at a constant 72°F—cold when it's 95° outside, pleasantly warm in winter. The state bought the site from a phosphate company in 1970 for $1.85 million and nothing's changed since. Entry $6 per vehicle, tube rental $7.50. Arrive before 10 AM in summer: the park closes once capacity hits 750 people, and that happens fast on weekends.

The absolute must-see, Blue Hole Spring requires a bit of effort—a half-mile walk from the North Entrance through a cypress forest. It's a first-magnitude spring, meaning flow exceeds 100 cubic feet per second. The pool descends 40 feet and opens into 600 feet of underwater caverns explored by technical divers. For casual snorkelers, it's already spectacular: sand boils up from the bottom like an inverted fountain. Avoid 2-4 PM—this is the one spot in the park that gets crowded.

If Florida and the Civil War seem incompatible, Olustee Battlefield will prove otherwise—February 20, 1864, 10,000 soldiers total engaged, Confederate victory, Florida's largest Civil War battle. The site has remained largely intact, with a one-mile interpretive trail. Annual reenactment in February draws the Southeast's biggest turnout. Free admission, open 8 AM to sunset. Twenty minutes east of Lake City, easy to combine with Ichetucknee if you have a full day.

activities.text: You float down the river in a tube from Dampier's Landing—0.75 miles, 45 minutes to an hour of gentle drifting through cypress trees and cruising turtles. The current does the work, you just hang on. Strictly prohibited: food, alcohol, single-use plastic, ice, non-reusable bottles—everything gets inspected at entry. Bring sunscreen (apply 30 minutes before entering the water to avoid polluting), reusable water bottle, water shoes.

Not exactly a culinary hotspot, Lake City—but Halpatter Brewing Company serves decent local IPAs and honest burgers in a rehabilitated 1902 railroad depot. Locals hang out here until late. For something more down-home, The Patio Place runs a classic Southern buffet (fried chicken, collard greens, mac & cheese) for $14—church cafeteria vibe, and that's exactly why you go.

visits.text: Black Point Estate - This Queen Anne mansion from 1888 was built by beer magnate Conrad Seipp as a summer residence. Accessible only by boat (the cruise is part of the experience). Twenty rooms furnished in period style, verandas overlooking the lake. It perfectly captures the Gilded Age when wealthy Chicago families escaped the city for Lake Geneva's shores.

Riviera Ballroom - This 1932 Art Deco building on the lakefront hosted the great swing-era orchestras. Today it serves as a performance venue and cruise departure point. The architecture is worth a stop even without a show.

Geneva Lake Shore Path - This 21-mile trail circles the entire lake passing in front of Gilded Age estates. You don't have to do it all: a 3-5 mile section is enough to see the finest properties and enjoy the views.

activities.text: Lake Geneva Cruise - Several cruise types: full lake tour (2h), mail boat cruise (the mailman jumps from the moving boat to deliver mail to lakefront property mailboxes - unique in the world), or sunset cruise.

visits.text: Lake Ouachita - Arkansas's Crystal-Clear Inland Sea: Spanning 40,000 acres with over 970 miles of pristine shoreline, this reservoir consistently ranks among America's cleanest lakes. Created by Blakely Mountain Dam, its impossibly clear waters reveal depths up to 40 feet, nestled among the forested Ouachita Mountains.

Garvan Woodland Gardens - 210 Acres of Botanical Paradise: Rising from a peninsula on Lake Hamilton, this University of Arkansas botanical garden transforms Ouachita forest into themed displays featuring the stunning Anthony Chapel, Asian garden, and America's largest bridge of its kind-all reflected in tranquil waters.

activities.text: Lake Ouachita Water Sports - Dive into Pure Mountain Water: The exceptional clarity supports world-class scuba diving revealing underwater rock formations, while kayakers, sailors, and anglers explore endless secluded coves surrounded by national forest.

Three Sisters Springs - Secret Turquoise Pools: Accessible only by boat, these natural springs create otherworldly blue pools where cold groundwater meets the lake, drawing snorkelers to their ethereal depths.

places.name: Lake Placid, NY

visits.text: Lake Placid is the only small American town to have hosted two Winter Olympics, in 1932 and 1980. The Olympic Center, right in town, houses the original rink of the "Miracle on Ice"—the impossible victory of the US amateur hockey team over the USSR on February 22, 1980. The ice is still there, you can walk on it between training sessions. Adjacent Olympic museum, $15. For sports fans, it's a pilgrimage.

The Intervales ski jumping complex is still used by the US team. The 90- and 120-meter jumps are visible from six miles away. An elevator goes up the big jump ($50) with 360° views over the Adirondacks. In summer, skiers train on jumps covered with wet synthetic material—surreal to watch them launch in 77°F weather.

Whiteface Mountain peaks at 4,867 feet and remains the only Olympic mountain in the East where you can drive to the summit. The five-mile Veterans Memorial Highway climbs to a parking lot at 4,430 feet, then a tunnel and elevator blasted through rock reach the summit in all weather. Built in 1935 under Roosevelt. Clear views to Mount Marcy, the state's highest point (5,344 feet). $18 per vehicle.

John Brown Farm, 1.8 miles from downtown Lake Placid, is the farm where abolitionist John Brown lived from 1849 until his hanging in 1859 after the Harpers Ferry raid. His body is buried here, along with those of several sons who fell in combat. State historic site, free. The wooden house remains almost as it was. Surprising to find such history in the heart of the Adirondacks—the region was an active abolitionist hub via the "Timbuctoo" colony.

High Falls Gorge in Wilmington (15 minutes east) features a suspended walkway system over the West Branch Ausable River. Four successive waterfalls, up to 60 feet high, along half a mile of circuit. Private, $18, open year-round (crampons provided in winter). Photogenic, short, accessible to fragile knees.

activities.text: Take a bobsled run down the Olympic track at Mount Van Hoevenberg. Summer or winter, you can launch at 60 mph with a pro driver for $125—the same track used by the national team. The experience lasts 50 seconds: brief, but unforgettable in the literal sense. Mandatory online reservation, 48 hours ahead.

Mirror Lake, smaller than Lake Placid but more central, offers a 2.5-mile walk around. Flat trail along the water, ideal in late afternoon. Kayak or paddleboard rental for $25-30/hour at the municipal dock. In winter, the free-access outdoor skating rink lights up until 10 pm—skates loaned for free.

Take a short hike around Cascade Lakes, 15 minutes from Lake Placid on Route 73. Easy 3-mile round-trip trail along two lakes wedged between cliffs—one of the most photographed Adirondacks spots in fall. Free roadside parking, but it fills by 8 am on weekends.

visits.text: Lake Tahoe — Marvel at North America's largest alpine lake spanning 496 square kilometers at 1,897 meters elevation. The impossibly blue waters reach 501 meters deep surrounded by Sierra Nevada peaks straddling the California-Nevada border.

Emerald Bay State Park — Photograph this fjord-like inlet featuring Fannette Island, Lake Tahoe's only island, topped by a stone teahouse. The scenic overlook offers the lake's most iconic vista with crystal waters framed by granite cliffs.

Sand Harbor — Swim in the clearest waters along massive granite boulders creating natural sculptures. This Nevada State Park beach offers white sand and turquoise waters rivaling tropical destinations.

Vikingsholm Castle — Tour this 1929 Scandinavian-style mansion built as summer retreat, considered finest example of Scandinavian architecture in the Western Hemisphere. The 38-room castle required 200 workers to construct on Emerald Bay's shores.

activities.text: Lake Tahoe Scenic Drive — Navigate 116 kilometers around the lake passing beaches, vista points, and forest. The route offers constantly changing mountain and water views.
Kayaking on crystal waters — Paddle across transparent waters allowing visibility to 21 meters depth. The lake's purity and dramatic shoreline create unforgettable paddling experiences.
Lakeside dining — Savor fresh trout and steaks at restaurants overlooking the sapphire waters. Tahoe's culinary scene emphasizes mountain cuisine with stunning views.

visits.text: You enter a 12-acre property that faithfully represents Amish life as it's still practiced today in Lancaster County. The guided tour of this 1840s farm takes you through the sparse rooms of a house without electricity, the forge, the one-room schoolhouse, the barn and its animals. The Amish began settling in this region in 1720, responding to William Penn's invitation that guaranteed religious freedom. Today, approximately 75,000 Amish live in Lancaster County, representing one of the largest communities in America. Book your tour in advance during high season; tours depart every 15 minutes, and allow at least three hours on site to also enjoy the bus tour through the back roads.

The Bird-in-Hand market is one of the most authentic in Amish country: you'll find hand-rolled pretzels, fresh cheeses, homemade jams, hand-stitched quilts, and locally crafted goods sold by Amish and Mennonite vendors. The village name - 'Bird-in-Hand' - supposedly comes from an 18th-century inn sign depicting a bird perched in a hand. On the roads between villages, it's common to pass Amish families in horse-drawn buggies, even on main roads - a sight that reminds you you've entered a different sense of time. The market is open Friday and Saturday year-round, with additional days in summer.

The Strasburg Rail Road is the oldest operating short-line railroad in the United States: its first operations date back to 1832, well before most American railroads existed. Your 45-minute ride aboard a steam locomotive takes you through the fields and farms of Amish country, with views of farmers in the fields and carriages waiting at grade crossings. The ticket includes round-trip from Strasburg station to Paradise, Pennsylvania - and yes, the village of Paradise actually exists. The Railroad Museum of Pennsylvania, right across from the station, houses one of the finest collections of historic locomotives in the country; allow an extra 45 minutes for a quick visit.

activities.text: Aaron & Jessica's Buggy Rides takes you along private paths through non-commercial Amish farms, where cars can't go. The drivers themselves belong to Amish and Mennonite communities, making the encounter direct and authentic. The draft horse, the slow pace, the clip-clop of hooves on asphalt, and the impeccably trimmed hedges around houses without power lines create total immersion in a way of life that 300 years of modernization haven't touched. A stop at a farm allows you to sample homemade cookies and lemonade. Go in the morning to catch the golden light on the fields and families starting their workday.

Kitchen Kettle Village in Intercourse - a village whose name invariably draws smiles from visitors - is the artisanal and culinary heart of Amish country. Since 1954, this collection of specialty shops has sold jams, apple butters, honeys, preserves, ceramics, and textiles made by local artisans. The Amish jam factory, visible from the shop, produces more than 100 varieties. The village also includes an inn, several restaurants, and a cheese shop. It's the best place to bring home authentic local products - prices are reasonable since you're buying directly from producers.

places.name: Lander, WY

visits.text: Six miles southwest of Lander on WY-131, the Middle Fork of the Popo Agie River pulls one of geology's stranger tricks: it disappears into a limestone cavern called 'the Sinks' and reappears a quarter mile downstream at 'the Rise' - taking more than two hours underground to cover that quarter mile. A paved path connects the two sites. At the Rise, a pool holds 8-12 pound rainbow trout protected from fishing since 1919; toss in food and the water churns. Humans have used this canyon for approximately 9,000 years. Free admission.

The Fremont County Pioneer Museum in downtown Lander anchors the town's founding logic: Lander was named for Frederick W. Lander, engineer of the Lander Trail used by thousands of westward emigrants. When the Chicago & North Western Transportation Company chose Lander as the western terminus of its 'Cowboy Line' railway in 1906, the phrase stuck - 'where the rails end and the trails begin.' It still fits today. Free admission.

Twenty-five miles south of Lander, Wild Iris is one of the best sport-climbing areas in North America - over 300 routes in bone-white dolomite limestone surrounded by aspen groves and wildflower meadows. Todd Skinner and partners first developed it in 1990. Even without climbing shoes, the drive alone is worth it: the meadows are spectacular in June and July, and Lander's International Climbers' Festival, running every July since 1994, is the longest-running climbing festival in the United States.

activities.text: The Canyon Loop Trail in Sinks Canyon crosses the river on a swinging bridge, loops past the Sinks and the Rise, then climbs the north wall for views across the limestone cliffs. The rock type shifts from sandstone to limestone to granite within a few miles as the Wind River Range closes in. Watch for bighorn sheep on the upper cliffs, mule deer in the canyon bottom, and moose near the river in early morning.

Main Street Lander in the evening has a working Western character unusual for a town of 7,500. Wild Iris Mountain Sports at 425 Popo Agie St is worth stopping in - staff have climbed every crag in the region and give genuine advice on the Wind Rivers. For dinner, Lander Brewing Company serves local craft beer alongside bison dishes; the Gannett Grill is the other local anchor.

visits.text: Stand at the Caesars Head overlook for endless views of Blue Ridge Mountain ridgelines and valleys stretching to the horizon. This dramatic granite outcrop provides some of the most spectacular mountain scenery in the entire state. The crisp mountain air and panoramic vistas make this a must-visit destination for nature lovers seeking awe-inspiring landscapes.

Hike to Raven Cliff Falls, the tallest waterfall in South Carolina, cascading dramatically over a 420-foot cliff. The approximately five-mile round-trip trail rewards hikers with one of the most impressive natural sights in the region. A suspension bridge on the Dismal Trail loop provides close-up views of the falls that few visitors forget.

activities.text: Squeeze through Devil's Kitchen, a quirky narrow rocky passageway leading toward the overlook that adds adventure to the mountain experience. The rugged trails, peaceful forests, and dramatic rock formations of Caesars Head State Park showcase the Blue Ridge at its finest. This mountain destination reminds visitors why escaping to the highlands feels so rejuvenating.

Explore Landrum's charming downtown, where rolling foothills, sweeping mountain views, and country roads lined with farms create an idyllic setting. Visit Pearson's Falls, a beautiful 90-foot waterfall tucked into a lush nature preserve, and hike the Blue Wall Preserve for stunning mountain panoramas. The area's equestrian culture adds distinctive character to this hidden gem.

places.name: Laramie, WY

visits.text: Built in 1872 as one of the few federal prisons of its time, the Wyoming Territorial Prison State Historic Site has sandstone walls that still feel oppressive. Of the 44 prisoners taken in during the first two years, 11 escaped. The most famous resident was Butch Cassidy, held here from 1894 to 1896 for grand larceny. After the prison moved to Rawlins in 1901, the University of Wyoming used the building as a livestock experiment station until 1989 - a strange afterlife for a place this grim. The site sits on 197 acres with a nature trail along the Big Laramie River. Fee applies; open Memorial Day through Labor Day.

A full Apatosaurus skeleton greets you near the entrance of the University of Wyoming Geological Museum - one of the more complete sauropod specimens on display anywhere in the state. The collection covers Wyoming's rich fossil record including dinosaur trackways and Morrison Formation specimens. Free admission. Allow 45-60 minutes; the historic Romanesque Revival campus buildings are worth a walk afterward.

At I-80 Exit 329, sixteen miles east of Laramie, the landscape breaks open into something that looks structurally impossible: 1.4 billion-year-old Sherman Granite stacked in towers up to 500 feet high. The Arapaho called this place 'bito'o'wu' - earth-born - a name popularized by a University of Wyoming drama professor in 1922. Over 900 climbing routes thread the rock; non-climbers can walk the 3.1-mile Turtle Rock Loop through aspen groves with minimal elevation gain. Day use fee applies.

activities.text: WY-130 west from Laramie is the day's main event - the Snowy Range Scenic Byway rises to 10,847 feet at Libby Flats, the second-highest mountain pass in Wyoming, designated the second National Forest Scenic Byway in 1988. Lake Marie is the best stop: Medicine Bow Peak (12,013 feet) appears to grow straight out of the water. At Libby Flats, views extend south into Colorado. If you're staying in Laramie tonight, make it an out-and-back; otherwise it's tomorrow's route to Saratoga.

Laramie's historic downtown repays an evening on foot - locally owned shops, colorful murals, and places like Range Leather Co. (handcrafted leather goods) and the Bent and Rusty (antiques and oddities). The town was born in 1868 when Union Pacific arrived; within months it had a population of several thousand. For dinner, try the Crowbar and Grill for hand-tossed pizza or Sweet Melissa for creative vegetarian dishes a block away.

visits.text: Walk the 400-foot square parade ground and you can see all nine original buildings surrounding you - something no comparable fort in the region can claim. Between 1866 and 1868, Captain A.F. Rockwell replaced the original sod-and-adobe structures with sandstone quarried locally, and every one of them still stands. Seven are open to visitors: barracks, officers' quarters, post hospital, blacksmith shop, commissary, and the commanding officer's quarters, all furnished to their 1860s-1870s appearance. The 10th U.S. Cavalry - one of the first two all-Black cavalry regiments in the Army - was stationed here from 1867 to 1869. Five miles southwest, original Santa Fe Trail wagon ruts remain visible in the prairie grass.

activities.text: Drive west from Lawrence on US-56 and you are on the route that traders followed from 1821 to 1872, moving goods between Missouri and Santa Fe, New Mexico. The land flattens dramatically west of Hillsboro. Consider a 15-minute detour to Pawnee Rock State Park, 9 miles northeast of Larned off US-56 - a sandstone prominence where Santa Fe Trail scouts watched for Comanche and Kiowa raiders, now free and open year-round with interpretive panels and views across the Arkansas River valley.

places.name: Las Vegas, NV

visits.text: Start with Ubehebe Crater (37.0089, -117.4519) before descending to Racetrack Playa—a volcanic crater 240 meters deep and 800 meters in diameter, formed by a phreatomagmatic explosion about 2,000 years ago when rising magma met an underground water table. The explosion hurled ash and rocks over a radius of several kilometers. Plunging view from the rim, permanent wind, descent into the crater possible in 20 minutes.

Leave early for Racetrack Playa (36.6800, -117.5642)—4x4 or Jeep mandatory for the 43 km of track from Ubehebe Crater, normal tires regularly punctured by sharp gravel. Rent a Jeep in Furnace Creek ($250-400/day) if you have a sedan. No cell signal: notify rangers before departure. The playa is a dried lakebed 4.5 km long, flat to within 2.5 cm across its entire surface—one of the flatest naturally occurring surfaces on Earth. On it sit dozens of stones, from pebbles to 320 kg boulders, each ending a long trail in the dried mud, sometimes over 200 meters. No one has ever seen a stone move. Yet they do.

The mystery of the moving stones lasted over 100 years. In December 2013, two geologists from Scripps Institution of Oceanography finally filmed the phenomenon with GPS and time-lapse cameras. Necessary conditions: winter rain creates 3-5 cm of water on the playa, a cold night forms a thin sheet of ice, morning sun melts the ice into large floating rafts, a light wind of 5-15 km/h pushes the rafts that encircle the stones and drag them across the soft mud. Result published in PLOS ONE in August 2014. End of mystery—the spectacle remains extraordinary.

Rise before dawn and go to Yavapai Point (36.0667, -112.1208) or Hopi Point (36.0728, -112.1542) for sunrise—35-40 minutes before to catch the raking light on the red layers. The Grand Canyon is 446 km long, up to 29 km wide, and 1,800 meters deep. The Colorado River took 6 million years to carve this canyon from a plateau initially flat at 2,100 meters. The 18 geological layers visible from the rim cover 1.75 billion years of Earth's history—from the Vishnu Schist at the bottom to the Kaibab Limestone under your feet. A cross-section of the planet.

Drive Hermit Road (36.062, -112.135)—11 km along the western rim, free shuttle mandatory March to November (cars prohibited). Nine viewpoints including Hopi Point, the most dramatic, with simultaneous views of 4 Colorado River meanders 1,800 meters below. Partially descend the Bright Angel Trail (36.0578, -112.1442)—2.4 km round-trip to the Mile-and-a-Half House, 320 meters elevation change, 2 to 3 hours. The descent is easy; the ascent in full sun is not: start before 9 AM and bring 2 liters of water minimum.

Before leaving, drive to Desert View Watchtower (36.0411, -111.8264)—35 km east of the visitor center, a 21-meter tower built in 1932 by architect Mary Colter in local stone, views of the narrower canyon and the Painted Desert beyond. Colter designed seven buildings in the park between 1905 and 1949, all still standing—her work is considered one of the most accomplished expressions of American vernacular architecture.

activities.text: Leave Death Valley late morning via CA-190 then NV-373 then I-15 to Las Vegas—2.5 hours drive. Two hundred kilometers of absolute desert, then suddenly a luminous city of 2.3 million inhabitants rises from the ground. The transition is surreal and deliberate: Las Vegas exists only because nothing exists around it. Arrival early afternoon.

First evening stroll on the Strip—the Bellagio fountains (36.1126, -115.1764) perform every 15-30 minutes, free, 3 to 5 minutes per show. The Conservatory & Botanical Gardens at Bellagio (36.1129, -115.1773), elaborate botanical gardens changing every 6 weeks, are free. Dine at a casino buffet—the Bacchanal at Caesars Palace for $50-80, or a neighborhood buffet for $15-30.

On the return route to Las Vegas, stop at Hoover Dam (36.0161, -114.7378)—an Art Deco dam from 1936, 221 meters high, that stops the Colorado and creates Lake Mead. The view from the bridge is free; the guided dam tour costs $30 and lasts one hour. Proof that the 1930s knew how to build infrastructure with aesthetic intention.

Arrive at Las Vegas LAS (36.0840, -115.1537) late afternoon for return flight—Paris via San Francisco, New York, Atlanta, or Amsterdam depending on options. Total car budget for the trip: $800-1,200 for 7 days one-way SF-Las Vegas rental, $70-150 one-way fees included.

visits.text: Lassen Volcanic National Park - The Only Place on Earth with All Four Volcano Types: Walk through a geothermal wonderland where the earth bubbles, hisses, and steams beneath your feet. This living laboratory showcases plug dome, shield, cinder cone, and composite volcanoes all within park boundaries.

Bumpass Hell - Three Miles into the Largest Hydrothermal Area in the Cascades: Follow the boardwalk trail past roaring fumaroles, bubbling mudpots, and scalding pools painted in otherworldly hues of orange, yellow, and turquoise. The trail honors Kendall Bumpass, who lost a leg when he broke through thin crust into boiling water.

Sulphur Works - Drive-Up Geothermal Theater: Steam vents and bubbling mud pools mere feet from the road offer the easiest access to the park's volcanic activity. The sulfurous smell announces your arrival before you see the first wisp of steam.

activities.text: Lassen Peak Summit Trail - Climb an Active Volcano: This 5-mile round-trip hike ascends 2,000 feet to the 10,457-foot summit, offering 360-degree views of the volcanic landscape. Lassen Peak last erupted in 1915, creating the devastated area still visible today.

places.name: Laurel, MS

visits.text: If you watch HGTV, you already know Laurel: it's the town from "Home Town" where Erin and Ben Napier have renovated houses since 2016—eight seasons and over 100 restored homes. Before the show, Laurel had dozens of empty buildings in its historic downtown. Today, fans make pilgrimages. The walkable downtown packs 80 shops into six blocks: Laurel Mercantile (the Napiers' store), Scotsman Co. (vintage furniture), bookstores, cafes. Everything's walkable in 2-3 hours.

A discreet Southern treasure, the Lauren Rogers Museum of Art was founded in 1923 by the Rogers family (timber industrialists) in memory of their son who died at 23. Permanent collection: American paintings (Sargent, Whistler, Homer, Cassatt), Dürer prints, the Southeast's largest collection of Native American baskets with 810 pieces. Free admission. The neoclassical marble building is as worth seeing as the art.

Do this on foot: North 5th Avenue, Magnolia Street, West Oak Street—downtown residential neighborhoods, Victorian houses and Craftsman bungalows perfectly restored, some visible in "Home Town." Gardens are maintained, porches occupied in late afternoon. Atmosphere of a real small Southern town, without the tourist fatigue of Charleston or Savannah. Free.

activities.text: Right next to the Napier studio, Pearl's Diner serves breakfast all day—biscuits-and-gravy, $5 pancakes. Otherwise, Café La Fleur in a renovated old house does more modern bistro cuisine (composed salads, gourmet sandwiches). And Slabtown Pizzeria for simple evenings.

visits.text: Walk six blocks from 6th Street to South Park and you are inside a National Register Historic District with 108 contributing properties, most built between 1856 and 1953. At 729-731, the House Building is the only commercial structure to survive Quantrill's 1863 raid intact. The Eldridge Hotel at 701-703 was Quantrill's main tactical target; the current five-story brick building dates from 1928, and each August 21 a white sheet is hung from a window to mark the anniversary. Free State Brewing Company at 636 Massachusetts opened in 1989 as the first legal brewery in Kansas in over a century.

You enter through the marble foyer of the 1888 Watkins National Bank Building at 1047 Massachusetts Street - marble staircases, stained-glass windows, and mosaic floors intact - and get the most thorough account of Quantrill's Raid in any Lawrence museum. The free permanent collection covers Douglas County history from Bleeding Kansas through the 20th century. James Patti's sculpture of Langston Hughes as a boy is here; Hughes grew up in Lawrence and based his 1930 novel Not Without Laughter on his childhood in this town.

Climb Mount Oread to the KU campus and you are on a National Historic District that opened in 1866 - one year after Quantrill's raid nearly prevented Lawrence from funding the new university at all. The Spencer Museum of Art (over 45,000 objects) and the KU Natural History Museum are both free and both worth at least 30 minutes each. James Naismith, the inventor of basketball and the only KU coach with a losing record, coached here and is buried in Lawrence.

activities.text: Download the free 1.5-mile self-guided walking tour from explorelawrence.com and follow Quantrill's path through 10 surviving sites - from South Park, where guerrillas staged their approach, to the Methodist Church that became a makeshift morgue by evening. The raid killed 20 percent of the town's male population and left 85 widows. Quantrill himself had lived in Lawrence under an alias and knew the town intimately before leading 450 men into it at dawn. The Watkins Museum also runs a paid Bleeding Kansas Bus Tour on select summer Saturdays for a wider sweep of the region.

End your day the way Lawrence does: with a pint and a plate on Mass Street. Free State Brewing Company has poured its flagship Ad Astra amber ale - named for the Kansas state motto, 'To the stars through difficulty' - since opening in 1989 as the first legal brewery in Kansas in over a century. For dinner, the Mad Greek at 9th and Massachusetts does flaming saganaki tableside. The Granada at 1020 Massachusetts, a Beaux-Arts venue that opened in 1912 with a 35-foot vaulted ceiling, hosts live music most nights under a chandelier the size of a small car.

visits.text: You enter a landscape where the granite is 550 million years old and the animals have been here - with a thirty-year gap - for over a century. The refuge was established July 4, 1901, making it the oldest facility in the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service system. On the roads you share space with free-roaming bison, Texas longhorn cattle (established on the refuge in 1927), Rocky Mountain elk (introduced from Jackson Hole, Wyoming, in 1908), white-tailed deer, and prairie dog towns. The Longhorn Trail - a 1.5-mile loop around French Lake - consistently produces bison and longhorn sightings. Drive at 15mph on all refuge roads; bison cross without warning and have the right of way in every sense.

You drive three miles of paved switchbacks to the summit of Mount Scott at 2,464 feet - the highest accessible point in the refuge - and step out into a 360-degree view of the granite-studded prairie below, Fort Sill to the south, and the wind farm on the Slick Hills to the north. The rock beneath your feet is part of the Mount Scott Granite, intruded roughly 530 million years ago. On a clear day you can see the curvature of the land. The drive takes about 20 minutes each way; stay for the full rim walk before heading back down.

You walk through a 66-acre granite complex inside the refuge built by WPA workers in 1934-35 to replicate biblical Jerusalem - Herod's Court, Pilate's judgment hall, the Garden of Gethsemane, watchtowers, and perimeter walls, all quarried from local rock with a $94,000 federal grant. It was built for the 'Prince of Peace' Easter passion play, which Rev. Anthony Mark Wallock first staged near Medicine Park in 1926 with five cast members and 200 attendees. Today it's the longest-running Easter pageant in the United States. A mile east, you find Medicine Park - a cobblestone resort village from 1908 where the buildings are faced with rounded granite pulled from local creek beds, and where legend holds that Al Capone kept a cabin. Both are free to visit.

activities.text: You push into 5,000 acres of designated wilderness where jumbled granite boulders and short cliff faces have drawn climbers since the 1960s and 70s. The Access Fund and Wichita Mountains Climbers Coalition maintain established routes on the rock faces. If you'd rather hike than climb, the 2.4-mile Sunset Trail crosses the wilderness to Treasure Lake - rocky underfoot, worth every step, but bring significantly more water than you think you need. There is no potable water anywhere on refuge trails, and summer heat in southwest Oklahoma will empty your bottles faster than any mountain trail.

You drive to a town of about a dozen people to eat a burger made from the animals you watched grazing this morning. The Meers Store has been here since 1901, and its 'Meersburger' uses longhorn beef culled annually from the refuge's own herd - the same Texas longhorns established on the refuge in 1927. The building looks like it was assembled over decades because it was. Meers is open Thursdays through Sundays only; arrive before 7pm or plan on a wait at the door.

visits.text: Deception Pass Bridge — Cross this dramatic 555-meter steel cantilever bridge connecting Whidbey Island to Fidalgo Island 55 meters above churning tidal waters. The 1935 structure frames views of rocky islands and forest-clad cliffs plunging to the sea.

Leavenworth Bavarian Village — Stroll this Alpine-themed town transformed in the 1960s with Bavarian architecture, beer gardens, and German restaurants. The former logging town reinvented itself as a tourist destination in the Cascade Mountains.

Waterfront Park — Walk along the Wenatchee River through this landscaped park featuring traditional German gazebos and gardens. The park hosts festivals year-round from Oktoberfest to Christmas lighting ceremonies.

Nutcracker Museum — View over 7,000 nutcrackers from around the world in this unique collection spanning six rooms. Examples range from medieval functional tools to ornate Bavarian figures and modern artistic interpretations.

activities.text: German cuisine sampling — Feast on schnitzel, bratwurst, spätzle, and apple strudel at authentic Bavarian restaurants complete with lederhosen-clad servers. Beer gardens serve German imports and local craft brews in festive atmosphere.

Icicle Gorge Trail hiking — Trek along the cascading Icicle Creek through old-growth forest and granite canyons. The relatively easy 4-mile trail offers swimming holes and dramatic mountain scenery in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

Wine tasting at local wineries — Sample Riesling, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir at tasting rooms surrounding Leavenworth. The Cascade foothills' elevation and temperature variations create favorable growing conditions.

visits.text: Stop at Tunnel View (37.7155, -119.6772) when entering Yosemite Valley—this is where the road emerges from the tunnel and El Capitan appears on the left, Bridalveil Fall on the right, Half Dome in the distance. Ansel Adams photographed this exact spot in 1934 and the image is one of the most reproduced in American history. El Capitan's granite monolith rises 2,308 meters and constitutes the world's largest continuous granite face—climbers who've free-soloed it since 2017 (Alexander Honnold) are visible to the naked eye from the parking lot.

Walk to Bridalveil Fall (37.7180, -119.6470) from its parking lot—5 minutes and 188 meters of waterfall before you, permanent mist in your face within 30 meters. Lower Yosemite Fall (37.7522, -119.5970) takes 30 minutes round-trip from the valley parking lot: 98 meters of drop, and in April-May the flow is so strong the sound is audible from 500 meters. The falls run dry in August-September.

Drive up to Glacier Point (37.7283, -119.5733) if the road is open (May-October only)—at 2,199 meters elevation, plunging view over the entire valley and Half Dome at eye level. This viewpoint radically changes your understanding of the canyon: you realize the valley is an 11 km glacial U carved between two 1,000-meter granite walls. The road is closed the rest of the year.

activities.text: Drive the Yosemite Valley Loop (37.745, -119.594) by free shuttle or car—19 km loop through the valley with views of all the peaks. Yosemite is 3.5-4 hours from San Francisco via I-580 and CA-120. Park ticket $35/vehicle for 7 days. Arrive before 10 AM or after 3 PM in high season to find parking in the valley.

Cross the Tioga Pass (CA-120 East, pass at 3,031 meters, the highest road pass in California) to reach Lee Vining in late afternoon. The road is closed in winter—check status at nps.gov before departing. One hour drive from the valley, with high Sierra Nevada landscapes opening progressively.

visits.text: You're wandering through one of Appalachia's best-preserved towns: 236 acres of Lewisburg's heart have been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1978, with Federal and Neoclassical houses dating from the late 18th century. The town was founded in 1782 by the Virginia Assembly, on a site occupied since 1751 by settlers near Lewis Spring. During the Civil War, the Battle of Lewisburg on May 23, 1862 saw Union forces under Colonel George Crook repel the Confederates - you can still see graffiti that soldiers from both sides carved into the walls of a building used as a hospital. In 2011, Frommer's Budget Travel named Lewisburg 'America's Coolest Small Town.'

You're walking through the door of one of only four Carnegie Halls still operating worldwide - there's of course one in New York, but also here, in an Appalachian town of 4,000 residents. Andrew Carnegie funded this neo-Georgian building in 1902 with a donation of $26,750 for the Lewisburg Female Institute, supplemented by $10,000 from the local community. When the college closed in 1972 and the building risked demolition, residents formed an association in 1983 and raised $3 million to save it. Today Carnegie Hall hosts concerts, exhibitions in three free galleries, and art classes year-round.

You're stopping before this gray stone church built in 1796, considered the oldest church building in continuous use west of the Alleghenies. It survived the Civil War because both armies used it in turn as a field hospital. The cemetery surrounding it dates partly from the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812; several officers from George Washington's army rest here. The interior, simple and white, retains its original oak pews. A quick visit suffices to grasp its atmosphere of historical quietude.

activities.text: You're setting out on one of the longest and most beautiful bike trails in Appalachia: 77 kilometers on the former Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad route, with an almost zero grade along the Greenbrier River. You're cycling between white limestone cliffs, green river meanders, and horse farms that have produced famous Greenbrier County beef for generations. The river has been renowned for trout fishing since the 19th century. Red brick railroad tunnels pierce the limestone ridges on certain sections.

You're descending into Lost World Caverns just north of Lewisburg and walking through a 500-meter underground gallery whose ceiling, 400 million years old, is covered with colossal stalactites and stalagmites. The showpiece is a 5-meter-tall stalagmite named 'Goliath,' one of the largest known specimens in Appalachia. The region sits on a Devonian limestone plateau riddled with underground caverns linked by active aquifer networks - Lost World Caverns is just one window into this system.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

visits.text: "The most historic square mile in America," Jimmy Carter said of Lewiston. A somewhat pompous formula, but not entirely unjustified for this village 15 minutes north of the falls. First European settlement in western New York State in 1720 (a French trading post called Le Magazin Royal), last stop on the Underground Railroad before crossing to Canada, site of the first American battle of the War of 1812. Center Street, the main artery, lines up 19th-century houses, art galleries, and over 30 restaurants in one kilometer.

The Freedom Crossing Monument, on the Niagara River shore, depicts a family of escaped enslaved people guided by an Underground Railroad agent toward the boat that will take them to Canada. Hundreds of people crossed the river here between 1820 and 1860 to escape slavery. Life-size bronze sculpture, explanatory plaques, free access. Moving, without descending into pathos.

The Niagara Power Vista, free admission, is the visitor center for the Robert Moses Power Plant, the world's largest hydroelectric plant when it opened January 28, 1961 (inaugurated by John F. Kennedy from the White House). 50 interactive exhibits explain how Niagara water is diverted through massive underground tunnels before the falls to power 13 turbines—mainly at night, to preserve the daytime spectacle. Plunging view of the gorge from the observation deck. One hour is enough, ideal for an educational finale.

activities.text: Whirlpool Jet Boat Tours, departing from the Lewiston dock: flat-bottom boats, 600 horsepower, that ascend the class V rapids of the lower gorge to the Niagara Whirlpool. Watertight option in covered boat or wet option—either way, it's an hour of thrills. Season May through October only; not recommended for children under six.

Final dinner on Center Street: the Brickyard Pub & BBQ for hickory-smoked ribs ($15 half portion), or Tin Pan Alley for more refined American cuisine. Both have been featured on Food Network, deservedly so. Digestive walk to the Tuscarora Heroes Monument, celebrating the Tuscarora warriors who saved civilian families during the British burning of Lewiston in December 1813. Journey ends on a strong historical note.

visits.text: Discover the Davidson County Historical Museum, housed in an elegant 19th-century Greek Revival building that provides an excellent opportunity to learn about Lexington's rich history and culture. The museum's fascinating exhibits chronicle the development of this charming Piedmont community through artifacts and historical displays.

Admire the stunning collection of works at the Bob Timberlake Gallery, celebrating one of North Carolina's most beloved artists. The gallery showcases Timberlake's masterful paintings capturing the essence of Southern rural life and the natural beauty of the Carolina landscape.

activities.text: Experience Lexington's lively winery scene, which offers plenty of opportunities to sample excellent local wines. The serene atmosphere at Childress Vineyards provides the perfect setting for tasting award-winning dry white wines while enjoying the beautiful rolling Piedmont countryside that surrounds this celebrated vineyard.
